26. Microservices Architecture & Patterns

At senior level the interesting question is never "what is a microservice?" but "should this be one, and what did it cost you?" Interviewers listen for trade-offs: microservices buy independent deployment and team autonomy, and they charge you in network failures, eventual consistency and operational work. This chapter uses RefinePoint as the worked example: 13 services plus a gateway, Kafka only where needed, and several patterns we chose not to adopt yet, with reasons.

26.1 Monolith, modular monolith, microservices

Monolith Modular monolith Microservices
Deployment One unit One unit Many units
Module boundary Convention Enforced in code (modules, ArchUnit, Spring Modulith) Network
Calls Method (ns) Method (ns) Network (ms, can fail)
Transactions ACID, simple ACID, simple Per service; saga across
Scaling Whole app Whole app Per service
Team autonomy Low at size Medium High
Operational cost Low Low High: tracing, discovery, CI per service
Refactoring across boundaries IDE rename IDE rename Versioned contract change

When NOT to use microservices: a small team, an unclear domain whose boundaries will move, no CI/CD or observability maturity, or no real need for independent scaling or deployment. Wrong boundaries are far more expensive across a network than inside one process. The default advice is valid: start with a well-structured modular monolith and extract when a concrete pressure appears (a module with a different scaling or release rhythm, or a team that keeps colliding).

RefinePoint: we are a solo-built product that did move to microservices, so we must be honest about why. The workload is genuinely uneven: run-service needs heap for DuckDB matching and scales by adding instances, while identity-service is small and busy. Billing and AI have different secrets and failure tolerance. An earlier single application was replaced with the same public API, and the rule since then is to extend a fitting service rather than create a new one. For a team of one the operational cost is real, and we pay for it with a shared platform library, one deploy script and one local start script.

26.2 Decomposition: business capability and bounded context

Decompose by business capability (what the business does: billing, reconciliation, notifications), not by technical layer ("database service") or entity ("customer service", which turns into a chatty CRUD wrapper). A bounded context (DDD) is the boundary inside which a term has one meaning: "Plan" means a subscription tier in billing, and nothing else elsewhere.

Signs of a good boundary: most changes touch one service, the data it needs is mostly its own, and it can do useful work when its neighbours are down.

Service Schema Owns
identity-service identity Workspaces, members, roles, invitations, API keys
billing-service billing Plans, subscriptions, Paddle, plan-limit checks
datasource-service datasource Data sources, connectors, file storage
reconciliation-service reconciliation Process definitions, visibility, data-quality rules
run-service run Running reconciliations, results, breaks, workflow, journals, exports
job-service jobs One-time and repeating jobs, schedules, execution history
ingest-service ingest File routing: uploads, API, SFTP inbox, inbound email
lookup-service lookup Workspace lookup tables, expression catalog
report-service report Reports and dashboards; reads others' data by asking the owner
ai-service ai AI assistance and AI settings
alert-notify-service alert_notify Alerts, email, webhooks
audit-service audit The audit log
instant-recon-service instant Airtable extension, instant reconciliations

26.3 Database per service

Each service owns its data, and others reach it only through its API or events. This gives independent schema evolution and prevents one service's query from harming another's data. A shared table is a hidden contract that nobody can change.

"Database per service" does not require a database server per service. Options in increasing isolation: separate schema with separate credentials, separate database, separate server.

RefinePoint: one Postgres server, one schema per service, and each service creates and migrates its own schema with Flyway at start-up. report-service has its own database user that owns only report, so it cannot read another schema even by mistake. It asks the owning service, as the caller. Moving a busy schema to its own server later is a configuration change, because no code joins across schemas.

26.4 Communication styles

Sync REST gRPC Async messaging
Coupling in time Both must be up Both must be up Consumer may be down
Payload JSON, verbose Protobuf, compact Any
Contract OpenAPI .proto, codegen Schema (Avro, JSON)
Streaming Awkward Built in (HTTP/2) Natural
Browser support Native Needs a proxy N/A
Consistency Immediate answer Immediate answer Eventual
Best for Public APIs, queries Internal low-latency, polyglot Fan-out, background work, buffering

Rule of thumb: use a sync call when the caller cannot continue without the answer, and an event when the producer does not care who reacts. A long synchronous chain multiplies failure: five services at 99.9% give about 99.5% overall (0.999⁵).

RefinePoint: API calls by default, Kafka only "when one event has several independent consumers, or must not be lost while its consumer is down." So rp.run.completed has two consumers (run counters in reconciliation, anomaly detection in ai) and a run must not wait for either, and rp.audit.events exists because recording an action must never fail because the audit service is down. Everything else is a plain HTTP call, which is simple to trace and debug.

26.5 API gateway

A single entry point that handles cross-cutting edge concerns: routing, TLS termination, CORS, authentication or its relay, rate limiting, request size limits, and aggregation.

Spring Cloud Gateway runs on WebFlux and Netty: a RoutePredicateHandlerMapping matches a route, then a FilteringWebHandler builds a chain from GlobalFilters and route GatewayFilters ordered by Ordered. It is non-blocking, so any blocking call in a filter stalls an event-loop thread and hurts every request.

spring.cloud.gateway.routes:
  - id: block-internal            # service-to-service endpoints are never exposed
    order: 0
    uri: no://op
    predicates: [ Path=/internal/** ]
    filters: [ SetStatus=404 ]
  - id: ai
    uri: ${RP_AI_URL:http://localhost:8108}
    predicates: [ "Path=/api/v1/organizations/*/ai/**,/api/v1/public/assistant/**" ]

RefinePoint: api-gateway does routing, CORS (including patterns for monday and Airtable origins), and rate limiting through a token-bucket RateLimitFilter keyed per API key, per user and per address. Note what it does not do: it does not authorise. It reads the token's sub claim without verifying the signature, only to pick a bucket; it passes the Authorization header through, and every service verifies the Keycloak token itself. So a bypassed or compromised gateway does not bypass authentication. Fat gateways holding business logic become a new monolith, so ours stops at routing, CORS and the limiter.

Authentication at the gateway vs in services: verifying at the edge only is simpler, but it leaves internal traffic trusted by position. Verifying in each service (zero-trust style) costs a little CPU per call but keeps each service safe on its own. Keys are cached locally, so JWT verification has no network hop.

26.6 Service discovery and configuration

Client-side Server-side
How Client asks the registry, picks an instance Client calls a stable address; a proxy or platform routes
Examples Eureka + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer Kubernetes Service (DNS + kube-proxy), AWS ALB
Load balancing In each client In the proxy
Language neutral No Yes

In Kubernetes you usually need no Eureka: http://run-service:8080 resolves through cluster DNS, and readiness probes remove unhealthy pods. Eureka is AP: registry data can be stale, so clients must handle dead instances. A service mesh (Istio, Linkerd) moves retries, mTLS and telemetry into sidecars.

Centralised configuration (Spring Cloud Config, Kubernetes ConfigMap/Secret, Vault): same artefact in every environment, values injected from outside, secrets separate, audit of changes, optional dynamic refresh (@RefreshScope).

RefinePoint: deliberately simple: no Eureka and no Kubernetes yet. Each service gets the base URL of each neighbour from configuration (rp.services.identity: http://...; RP_*_URL for the gateway), one systemd unit template runs the jars, and nginx fronts the gateway. "A server differs from another only in its /etc/refinepoint/*.env: the jars are the same everywhere." PlatformDefaults supplies shared defaults so a service's own YAML stays small. When instances multiply beyond what fixed URLs handle, Kubernetes DNS replaces this without any code change.

26.7 Resilience patterns

Failures in a distributed system are normal. The most dangerous one is not a crash but a slow dependency: requests pile up, threads and pool connections run out, and the failure spreads to callers.

Timeouts come first: every remote call needs a connect and a read timeout, and a caller's timeout should be longer than the sum it depends on, or be propagated as a deadline.

Retries only for transient errors, only for idempotent operations, with exponential backoff and jitter, and a limit. Without jitter all clients retry in lockstep. Retries at each of three layers multiply: 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 calls on the bottom service, a self-made DDoS. Retry at one layer and use a retry budget.

delay = min(cap, base × 2^attempt)            exponential
sleep = random(0, delay)                      full jitter

Circuit breaker stops calling a dependency that keeps failing, so it fails fast and gives the dependency room to recover.

@CircuitBreaker(name = "billing", fallbackMethod = "lastKnownPlan")
@Retry(name = "billing")
@Bulkhead(name = "billing")
public Plan planOf(UUID orgId) { return billingClient.plan(orgId); }

Plan lastKnownPlan(UUID orgId, Throwable t) { return planCache.lastKnown(orgId); }
resilience4j.circuitbreaker.instances.billing:
  sliding-window-type: COUNT_BASED
  sliding-window-size: 50
  minimum-number-of-calls: 20
  failure-rate-threshold: 50
  slow-call-duration-threshold: 2s
  slow-call-rate-threshold: 80
  wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s
  permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 5
resilience4j.retry.instances.billing:
  max-attempts: 3
  wait-duration: 200ms
  enable-exponential-backoff: true
  enable-randomized-wait: true

Aspect order defaults to Retry(CircuitBreaker(RateLimiter(TimeLimiter(Bulkhead(fn))))), so the retry wraps the breaker, and an open breaker's rejection should not be retried.

Pattern Protects against Mechanism
Timeout Hanging dependency Bound the wait
Retry Transient glitch Try again, with backoff and jitter
Circuit breaker Persistent failure Fail fast, probe later
Bulkhead One dependency consuming all threads Separate semaphore or thread pool per dependency
Rate limiter Overload Reject over a rate, usually with 429
Fallback Loss of a feature Cached, default or degraded answer
Load shedding Saturation Reject early, protect the core

Fallbacks must be honest. A "default" that hides a failure can be worse than an error: falling back to "free plan" could lock out a paying customer.

RefinePoint: every internal call goes through InternalClient, with a 2-second connect and 10-second read timeout; an unreachable service becomes a RemoteCallException (503). We do not run Resilience4j yet, and we should say so plainly. Instead we reduce the blast radius by design: audit and run-completed events go through an outbox, access answers are cached for 30 seconds, and failed jobs retry with doubling backoff in job-service. A circuit breaker on identity and billing calls is the natural next step as traffic grows.

26.8 Idempotency

An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect. Any at-least-once system (HTTP retries, Kafka redelivery, webhooks) needs it.

  • HTTP: GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent by contract, POST is not. Use an Idempotency-Key header: store key + response in a unique-constrained table, in the same transaction as the work, and return the saved response on a repeat.
  • Natural keys: UNIQUE (org_id, external_ref) + ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING.
  • Absolute state rather than deltas: "set status to PAID" repeats safely, "add 100" does not.
  • Version checks: ignore an event whose version is older than the stored one.

26.9 Saga: transactions across services

Two-phase commit does not fit microservices: it blocks on a coordinator, needs XA support (Kafka and most NoSQL lack it), and couples availability. A saga is a sequence of local transactions, where each failure triggers compensating transactions for the completed steps. There is no isolation between steps, so other transactions can see intermediate states.

Choreography Orchestration
Control Services react to events Central orchestrator commands
Coupling Loose, but flow is implicit To the orchestrator, flow is explicit
Understanding the flow Hard past 3–4 steps One place, one state machine
Failure handling Scattered Centralised, with timeouts
Risk Cyclic events Orchestrator becoming a god service
Tools Kafka Temporal, Camunda, a state table

Handling the lack of isolation: semantic locks (a PENDING status), commutative updates, re-reading before acting, and putting the steps that are hard to compensate (sending an email, taking a payment) last. Every step and compensation must be idempotent and retryable; a compensation is not an "undo" (a refund is a new business action).

RefinePoint: we have no multi-step distributed saga, because our boundaries avoid needing one: a run's matching and result writes stay in one service. Our closest long flow is simple orchestration: job-service's DataRetentionJob asks billing how long a plan keeps results, asks reconciliation what the close holds, and then tells run to purge. Saying "we don't need one and here's why" is a stronger answer than inventing one.

26.10 Transactional outbox, CDC and the inbox

The dual-write problem: save(entity); kafka.send(event); can fail between the two. Commit then crash → event lost. Send then rollback → event for something that never happened. No transaction spans Postgres and Kafka.

Outbox: write the event into an outbox_events table in the same transaction as the business change, and have a separate process publish it.

sent = tx.execute(status -> sendBatch());   // one transaction per batch of 100
// per row: kafka.send(...).get(10, SECONDS), then UPDATE ... SET sent_at = now()
// on failure: record attempts + last_error, break  -> retried next tick, in order
@KafkaListener(topics = "#{topics.runCompleted()}")
@Transactional
void on(String message) {
    EventEnvelope e = consumed.parse(message);
    if (e == null || !consumed.firstTime("run-counter", e.id())) return;  // bad or repeat
    counters.increment(consumed.payload(e, RunCompleted.class));          // same tx as the dedupe row
}

Because the dedupe row and the business effect commit together, a crash replays cleanly: either both are there, or neither is.

Polling relay (ours) CDC with Debezium
How Scheduled SELECT Reads the WAL via logical decoding
Latency Polling interval (1 s) Very low
Infrastructure None beyond DB + Kafka Kafka Connect, replication slot to monitor
Load on the DB Query per tick Low, but an abandoned slot retains WAL and fills the disk
Order Ours, from seq Commit order per table/partition

With Debezium you still prefer an outbox table (its Outbox Event Router) over raw table CDC, because raw CDC publishes your internal schema as a public contract.

RefinePoint: OutboxRelay lives in ryfn-platform, so every service has it. A failed send stops the batch and retries next tick, and purge() keeps tables small (sent events gone after 7 days, consumed ids after 30). ConsumedEvents.parse logs and skips a malformed message so one poison message cannot block a topic. One honest limit: with several instances, SKIP LOCKED batches can overlap in time, so order is strict per relay instance, not globally. Consumers must tolerate reordering as well as duplicates.

26.11 CQRS and event sourcing

CQRS separates the write model (validates commands, keeps invariants) from read models (denormalised and optimised per query). The levels range from separate DTO queries on the same tables, through a replica, to a separate store fed by events. It pays off when reads and writes differ greatly, at the cost of eventual consistency and duplicate data.

Event sourcing stores the sequence of events as the source of truth; current state is a replay (with snapshots for speed). Gains: a complete audit trail, time travel, new projections from history. Costs: event schema evolution forever (upcasters), replays, harder GDPR deletion (crypto-shredding), a steep learning curve. CQRS and event sourcing are independent: you can use one without the other. Use event sourcing where history is the domain (ledgers), not by default.

RefinePoint: we store current state plus an audit log rather than event sourcing: rp.audit.events feeds audit-service, which records what happened, but the audit log is not what rebuilds state. Each run's results sit in dedicated per-run tables, a read-optimised structure with its own archive path.

26.12 API composition, BFF, and reporting across services

API composition: a composer (gateway, BFF or service) calls several services and joins the results in memory. It is simple but bounded by the slowest service, weak on large joins, and needs partial-failure rules. BFF (Backend for Frontend) gives each client type its own API layer that fits its screens, owned by the front-end team; it must hold no business rules.

Reporting across services has no cross-schema JOIN. Options: API composition (small data); CQRS read model built from events; data warehouse fed by CDC or batch (for analytics).

RefinePoint: report-service is read-only over other services' data and asks each owner as the caller (asCaller), so a report can never show what its user may not see. This is API composition, which is enough today; if reports ever need heavy joins across large data, an event-fed read model or warehouse is the next step.

26.13 Strangler fig migration

Put a routing layer in front of the monolith and move capabilities out one at a time while the client contract stays the same; when nothing remains, remove the monolith.

Steps: add the facade, pick a low-risk seam, copy or sync the data (dual writes or CDC), shadow traffic and compare, switch the route with a rollback option, delete the old code. Use an anti-corruption layer so the old model does not leak in. Database decoupling is usually the hardest part.

RefinePoint: the earlier single application was replaced behind an unchanged contract: "the same paths, on the same port (8082), with the same responses." Clients did not change, and that is why the gateway's route list is organised by path prefix, with explicit "exceptions that sit under another service's prefix" ordered first. Having no production data made the move simple, which is exactly the part a real migration cannot skip.

26.14 Tracing, correlation and observability

One request spans many services, so logs per service are not enough. Trace = the whole request; span = one operation, carrying a trace id, a span id and a parent id. W3C traceparent propagates the context over HTTP and in message headers. Micrometer Tracing + OpenTelemetry exports spans over OTLP to Tempo or Jaeger. Sampling keeps cost down: head sampling decides up front, tail sampling keeps errors and slow traces.

The three pillars: logs (with trace id via MDC), metrics (RED: rate, errors, duration; USE for resources), traces. Async boundaries need the trace context carried in message headers, or the trace breaks. Note that in @Async and virtual-thread handoffs MDC does not carry over automatically.

RefinePoint: PlatformObservabilityAutoConfiguration gives every service this for free: "every request, internal call and Kafka event carries a W3C traceparent," with trace and span ids in each log line, Prometheus metrics, default sampling of 10% (TRACING_SAMPLING), and spans exported only when an OTLP endpoint is configured.

26.15 Service-to-service security

Option What it proves Trade-offs
Shared internal token "I hold the cluster secret" Simple; one leak exposes all; no per-service identity
OAuth2 client credentials Service identity + scopes, via a JWT Standard; adds token handling and an auth server dependency
Forward the user's JWT The original user's rights Keeps permission checks; short token lifetime hurts long jobs
mTLS Both ends' identities, encrypted link Certificate rotation; usually delegated to a mesh

RefinePoint: InternalClient has two flavours. system("run") sends only X-Internal-Token, for schedules and event handlers. asCaller("run") also forwards the user's bearer token or API key and the workspace header, so the receiver checks permissions as for a direct request, and "the AI service, reading results for a user, never sees more than that user could." InternalTokenFilter guards /internal/** with a constant-time compare (Hashing.sameSecret), and the gateway answers /internal/** with 404. A shared token is the known weak spot; per-service identity through mTLS or client credentials is the upgrade once we leave one trusted host network.

26.16 Versioning, contracts and deployment

Backward compatibility is what lets services deploy independently. Safe changes: adding optional fields or new endpoints. Consumers must be tolerant readers (ignore unknown fields). Breaking changes: removing or renaming fields, tightening validation, changing meaning. Versioning styles: path (/api/v1, simplest and visible), header or media type (cleaner URLs, harder to test). Run the old and new versions side by side, and retire the old by watching usage. Events follow the same rules, with a schema registry and compatibility modes (BACKWARD, FORWARD, FULL).

Contract testing (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract) verifies provider and consumer agree without standing up the whole system: consumers publish expectations, and the provider's CI verifies them, catching breaks before deployment. It is cheaper and less flaky than end-to-end tests.

Strategy Mechanism Rollback Cost Mixed versions?
Rolling Replace instances gradually Slow, roll forward Low Yes
Blue-green Two full environments, switch traffic Instant Double capacity No (except DB)
Canary Small % first, watch metrics Fast Medium, needs traffic split Yes
Feature flag Deploy dark, release by flag Instant Flag debt Code only

Database changes must always be backward compatible (expand/contract, chapter 24), because old and new code will run together. Graceful shutdown matters too: stop taking traffic, finish in-flight work (server.shutdown=graceful).

RefinePoint: deployment is per-service and selective: ONLY="run billing" (or the tick list in deploy-pick.sh) ships just those jars and restarts them, while a full deploy covers all services. End-to-end tests live in ryfn-deploy. Path versioning is /api/v1, and the event envelope is shared through the platform library.

Factor Meaning RefinePoint
Codebase One repo per app, many deploys One repo per service
Dependencies Declared, isolated Maven; executable jars
Config In the environment /etc/refinepoint/*.env
Backing services Attached resources Postgres, Kafka by URL
Build, release, run Strict separation Same jar for every server
Processes Stateless Queue in the DB; any instance takes work
Port binding Self-contained Embedded server per service
Concurrency Scale by processes More run-service instances
Disposability Fast start, graceful stop Heartbeat and re-queue of a dead worker's runs
Dev/prod parity Similar environments start-local.sh runs the same stack
Logs Event streams Log lines carrying trace ids
Admin processes One-offs Flyway migrates at start; job-service for batch

26.18 Shared libraries vs duplication

A shared library saves repeated code, but creates binary coupling: every upgrade requires rebuilding consumers, and a fat library becomes a distributed monolith's backbone. Share infrastructure (security wiring, envelope, outbox, logging), never domain logic. Keep it versioned, backward compatible and small; duplicate small things rather than couple services (DRY applies within a boundary).

RefinePoint: ryfn-platform holds auto-configurations (PlatformSecurityAutoConfiguration, PlatformEventsAutoConfiguration, PlatformWebAutoConfiguration, observability, OpenAPI), ApiResponse, GlobalExceptionHandler, BaseEntity/BaseOrgEntity, InternalClient, SlidingWindowLimiter, TtlCache. Result: a new service gets security, envelope, tracing and outbox with one dependency. The cost is real, and our gotcha is the clean build: a service's jar embeds the platform jar it was built with, so after editing ryfn-platform, you must mvn clean package every service. A service you skipped keeps running the old platform code. That is a silent version split between services, the essence of the shared-library trade-off. With a team, we would publish versioned releases and enforce compatibility in CI.

26.19 Multi-tenancy across services

Model Isolation Cost per tenant Operations
Shared schema, org_id column Application-enforced Lowest One migration; noisy neighbours
Schema per tenant Better Medium Migrate N schemas
Database per tenant Best Highest Many pools; many migrations

In microservices tenant context must flow across calls: path or header at the edge, verified against the caller's memberships, forwarded on internal calls, included in events, and used by every query and cache key. Also handle fairness: per-tenant rate limits and concurrency caps, so one tenant cannot starve the others.

RefinePoint: org-scoped paths and X-Org-Code; OrgAccessInterceptor/OrgContextService set the context; BaseOrgEntity puts org_id on every tenant table; asCaller forwards the workspace header; the run queue applies a per-workspace cap on concurrent runs; PlanLimits enforces plan limits from billing.

26.20 Common failures

Anti-pattern Symptom Fix
Distributed monolith Must deploy services together; a shared DB or fat library Fix boundaries, contracts, compatibility
Chatty services Dozens of calls per request; N+1 over HTTP Bulk endpoints, merge services, cache
Cascading failure One slow service takes the rest down Timeouts, bulkheads, breakers, load shedding
Shared database A column rename breaks other teams Ownership, API, schema credentials
Sync chains Latency and failure multiply Async, data replication, redesign
Too many, too soon More services than people Merge; a modular monolith
No observability Hours to find where a request failed Traces and correlation from day one

26.21 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is a microservice, in one sentence?

An independently deployable service, built around one business capability, that owns its data and communicates only through well-defined contracts. Independent deployment is the test: if you must release services together, you have a distributed monolith, however small each one is. Size is not the point.

Q2. When would you advise against microservices?

For a small team, an early product with unclear boundaries, or a system with no real differences in scaling or release rhythm, I would advise a modular monolith. Microservices buy team autonomy at the price of network failures, eventual consistency and operational overhead. If you have no CI/CD and tracing, they make everything harder. The cost arrives on day one; the benefit arrives with scale.

Q3. What is a modular monolith and why is it often the better start?

One deployable with strictly enforced module boundaries (package rules, ArchUnit, Spring Modulith, events between modules). You get cheap refactoring and ACID transactions while discovering the real boundaries, and a clean module is later easy to extract. Moving a boundary is an IDE refactor rather than a coordinated contract change.

Q4. How do you identify service boundaries?

Start from business capabilities and DDD bounded contexts (event storming helps), then test them: does a typical change touch one service, can it own its data, can it do something useful when neighbours are down? Look at data that changes together and terms whose meaning changes between areas. Also weigh pragmatic forces like different scaling needs, compliance or team structure (Conway's law).

Q5. How were RefinePoint's service boundaries chosen?

By capability, and refined by workload. Definitions (reconciliation-service) are separated from execution (run-service) because they differ in load: a run needs heap and DuckDB, and is scaled by adding instances, while editing a definition is light. Identity, billing and audit are separate because of their sensitivity and failure tolerance. New features extend a fitting service rather than creating another, because 13 is already a lot for one person.

Q6. Why is a shared database an anti-pattern?

Because the schema becomes a hidden contract between services: nobody can rename a column without coordinating, one service's heavy query or lock affects others, and ownership of invariants blurs. Sharing a database server with separate schemas and credentials is fine; sharing tables is the problem. We enforce this with separate schemas, and report-service's user can only reach report.

Q7. How do you get data another service owns?

Ask it through its API (simple, always fresh, adds a runtime dependency), subscribe to its events and keep a local copy (fast and independent, eventually consistent), or combine with a short-lived cache. The right choice depends on freshness needs and call volume. RefinePoint asks identity for roles and keeps the answer for 30 seconds, and reads lookup tables once per minute through RemoteLookupSource, so a run that looks up every row asks only once.

Q8. REST vs gRPC vs messaging?

REST for public APIs and simple internal calls; gRPC for low-latency internal calls, streaming and polyglot typed contracts; messaging when the caller need not wait, several consumers react, or the consumer may be down. It is not an either/or at system level. Use a sync call when you need the answer to continue, an event when you are announcing something that happened.

Q9. Command vs event messages?

A command asks one recipient to do something (SendInvoice), can be refused, and couples the sender to the receiver's capability. An event states a fact that happened (RunCompleted), has any number of consumers and cannot be refused. Events invert the dependency: the producer does not know the consumers. rp.run.completed means run-service knows nothing of the anomaly detector.

Q10. What does an API gateway do, and what should it not do?

It is the single entry point for routing, TLS, CORS, rate limiting, authentication relay and sometimes response aggregation. It should not hold business rules or per-domain data transformations, or it becomes a new monolith that every team must queue to change. Keep it boring, and scale it horizontally because it is a critical path.

Q11. How does Spring Cloud Gateway process a request?

RoutePredicateHandlerMapping finds the first route whose predicates match. FilteringWebHandler builds a chain of global and route filters sorted by order. NettyRoutingFilter proxies the request non-blockingly, and the post part of the filters runs on the response. It runs on WebFlux, so blocking calls in filters are a serious bug, as they stall event-loop threads.

Q12. Should the gateway validate JWTs or should services?

Both are defensible; I prefer services verifying themselves, optionally with the gateway rejecting obviously invalid tokens early. Edge-only validation means anything inside the network is trusted. Signature checking is local (cached JWKS), so it costs little. RefinePoint's gateway only reads the sub claim to choose a rate-limit bucket, unverified. A forged sub gets its own bucket, the per-address bucket still counts it, and the service then rejects the token.

Q13. Client-side vs server-side discovery?

With client-side discovery (Eureka + Spring Cloud LoadBalancer) the client gets instances from the registry and picks one, which is flexible but language-specific. With server-side discovery (Kubernetes Service, ALB) the client calls a stable name and the platform routes it. In Kubernetes, DNS plus readiness probes are usually enough, and adding Eureka only duplicates them.

Q14. How do you manage configuration across many services?

Externalise it: one artefact for all environments, values from the environment or a config service, secrets in a vault or secret manager, and defaults in code. Avoid scattered copies, and be careful with runtime refresh of things that are not safe to change live. For RefinePoint: per-server env files and PlatformDefaults shared defaults, without a config server, since fewer moving parts suit a single operator.

Q15. What timeouts would you set on service calls?

Connect short (1–2 s), read from the dependency's real p99 plus margin, and keep the outer timeout larger than the inner one, or pass a deadline down the chain. Unbounded default timeouts are the commonest cause of cascading failure. In InternalClient we use 2 s and 10 s as global defaults. A stricter design would tune per dependency and propagate the remaining deadline.

Q16. Retry rules: when and how?

Retry only transient failures (timeouts, 503, connection reset), only idempotent operations, with exponential backoff and jitter, a small attempt limit and at one layer. Never retry 4xx validation errors. Honour Retry-After on 429. Retrying a non-idempotent POST needs an idempotency key, otherwise a timed-out but successful request is applied twice.

Q17. What is a retry storm?

Retries at each layer multiply load exactly when a dependency is struggling: 3 attempts at each of 3 layers is 27 calls on the bottom service, so a brief slowdown becomes an outage. Prevent it with one retry layer, a retry budget (say, retries at most 10% of traffic), jitter, and circuit breakers that stop retries when the dependency is unhealthy.

Q18. Explain circuit breaker states.

Closed: calls pass and results are recorded in a sliding window. Open: when the failure or slow-call rate crosses the threshold, calls fail immediately for a wait period, which protects both sides. Half-open: a few trial calls decide between closing and reopening. Tune minimumNumberOfCalls so one early failure does not trip it, and count slow calls as failures, because slowness does the most damage.

Q19. Which exceptions should count as circuit-breaker failures?

Infrastructure failures such as timeouts, connection errors and 5xx. A 404 or a validation error means the dependency is healthy, so counting it would open the breaker for a client mistake. Configure recordExceptions/ignoreExceptions accordingly. Similarly an open-circuit rejection should not be retried.

Q20. Circuit breaker vs retry vs bulkhead?

Retry handles short glitches by trying again. A circuit breaker handles sustained failure by not trying. A bulkhead limits concurrent calls per dependency, so one slow dependency cannot consume every thread. They compose: bulkhead limits the concurrency, the breaker stops calls to a sick dependency, and retry handles the rare blip. Timeouts sit beneath all of them.

Q21. How do virtual threads change bulkheads?

Thread exhaustion stops being the main risk, as virtual threads are nearly free, so a slow dependency no longer starves a pool of request threads. But you can now hit the database pool or the downstream service with far more concurrency, so limits must become explicit semaphores. Bulkheads become more important, not less, and their form changes from thread pool to semaphore.

Q22. Your service is failing because a downstream is slow. Walk through what is happening.

Requests wait on the downstream, holding threads and pool connections; the pool empties, new requests queue, latency rises, health checks may fail, and the orchestrator might restart instances, adding load. Callers then time out and retry, making it worse. Immediate action: shed load or open the breaker, and shorten timeouts. Long term: bulkheads, async where possible, per-dependency limits, and alerts on saturation rather than only on errors.

Q23. What is a good fallback? Give a bad one.

Good: cached last-known data clearly acceptable for that use, a reduced feature (hide recommendations), or a queued request. Bad: silently returning a default that changes a decision, such as treating a billing failure as "free plan", or treating an access-check failure as "allowed". Security and money checks should fail closed.

Q24. How do you make a POST idempotent?

The client sends a unique Idempotency-Key; the server stores it in a table with a unique constraint, in the same transaction as the work, along with the response. A repeat returns the saved response, and a concurrent duplicate hits the constraint and waits or gets a 409. Keys are scoped per tenant and expire. Paddle-style webhooks use the provider's event id the same way.

Q25. Why doesn't two-phase commit suit microservices?

It holds locks across services while waiting for a coordinator, so availability and latency become the product of all participants; a coordinator failure leaves participants in doubt. Most modern components, like Kafka and many NoSQL stores, do not support XA. Each service would also be tied to one transaction protocol. Sagas exchange atomicity and isolation for availability and autonomy.

Q26. What is a saga? Choreography vs orchestration?

A sequence of local transactions with compensating actions on failure. In choreography, each service reacts to events, which is loosely coupled but makes the flow implicit and hard to follow past a few steps. In orchestration, a central state machine sends commands, so the flow is explicit and observable, at the cost of a coordinating component. I use choreography for short flows and orchestration when there are many steps or business people care about the state.

Q27. What are the weaknesses of sagas, and how do you handle missing isolation?

Other transactions can read intermediate states (dirty reads) or lose updates, and compensations can themselves fail. Countermeasures: semantic locks through a PENDING status, commutative updates, re-reading values before acting, ordering so that hard-to-compensate steps run last (pivot transaction), idempotent and retried compensations, and a dead-letter route with human handling as the last resort.

Q28. What is the dual-write problem?

Writing to two systems, usually the database and a broker, with no shared transaction, so a crash between them makes them disagree: the event is lost or describes something that rolled back. @Transactional does not help, since Kafka is not in the DB transaction; sending inside the transaction can publish before a commit that later fails. The solution is the outbox, CDC or event sourcing.

Q29. Explain the transactional outbox and walk through a failure.

The event is inserted in the same transaction as the business change, then a relay publishes it. If the service crashes before commit, both are gone: consistent. If it crashes after commit, the relay publishes later. If the relay crashes after Kafka acknowledges but before marking sent_at, the next tick resends. So delivery is at least once, never lost, and consumers must dedupe. In RefinePoint this is OutboxRelay with seq order and SKIP LOCKED.

Q30. Why does your relay stop the batch on a failure?

To keep order: if event 5 fails and 6 is sent, a consumer can see them inverted. Stopping leaves everything from 5 onward for the next tick, and attempts and last_error are recorded on the row. The trade-off is that a permanently failing event would block those behind it, so alert on old unsent rows. Note this keeps order per relay instance. Two instances with SKIP LOCKED can interleave batches, so consumers should not assume global ordering.

Q31. How do you guarantee ordering in Kafka with an outbox?

Kafka orders per partition, so use a key (the aggregate id) for events that must stay ordered, as event_key does, and enable an idempotent producer. A single relay, or partitioned relays per key, preserves order. Otherwise treat order as best effort and make consumers robust: compare a version on the event and ignore anything older than the stored state.

Q32. Polling outbox vs Debezium?

Polling is simple: no new infrastructure, easy to reason about, a cost in latency (our default is one second) and in query load. Debezium reads the WAL with very low latency and little DB load, but brings Kafka Connect and a replication slot that can fill the disk if it stalls. I would start with polling and move to CDC when volume or latency requires it.

Q33. What is the idempotent consumer (inbox) pattern?

The consumer records each processed event id in a table with a unique key, in the same transaction as its effect, and skips repeats. In RefinePoint: ConsumedEvents.firstTime(consumer, eventId) runs INSERT … ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING and returns whether a row was inserted. The consumer name is part of the key, so different consumers in a service each process the event. Ids are purged after 30 days, which must exceed any possible redelivery window.

Q34. Exactly-once delivery: is it possible?

Exactly-once delivery across arbitrary systems is not; exactly-once effect is, through at-least-once delivery plus idempotent processing. Kafka's transactions provide exactly-once semantics inside Kafka (read-process-write between topics), but an external side effect such as a database write or an email still needs dedupe. Saying this clearly is what the interviewer wants to hear.

Q35. How do you handle a poison message?

Limit retries, then send it to a dead-letter topic with error metadata, alert, and provide a replay path after a fix. Do not let it block a partition indefinitely. Spring Kafka's DefaultErrorHandler with DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer does this. RefinePoint's ConsumedEvents.parse already logs and skips unreadable envelopes so that a malformed message cannot block the topic.

Q36. What is CQRS? When is it overkill?

Separate models for writes and reads, optionally separate stores synchronised by events. It helps when read shapes differ greatly from the write model, or reads vastly outnumber writes. It is overkill for CRUD: you pay with eventual consistency and synchronisation code. A lightweight form, read-only DTO queries over the same tables with JdbcTemplate on hot paths, is often all you need, and that is what we do.

Q37. What is event sourcing? Would you use it for reconciliation?

State is derived by replaying an immutable event log, giving full history and new projections from old data, at the cost of event versioning forever, snapshots, and harder queries. For the ledger or approval trail of a reconciliation it is tempting, but we get what auditors need from an audit log plus per-run stored results, with much less complexity. I would adopt it only where history is the primary query.

Q38. How do you do a read across services for a screen?

API composition in a BFF or the aggregating service with parallel calls, when data is small and partial failure is tolerable. Otherwise maintain a denormalised read model from events. Avoid N+1 over HTTP by offering bulk endpoints (GET /users?ids=...). Fetching in parallel is easy with Java 21 virtual threads, with explicit timeouts.

Q39. What is a BFF, and why not a general gateway?

A Backend for Frontend tailors the API to one client type: a mobile screen wants a few aggregated fields, a desktop grid wants many. It avoids over-fetching and keeps client-specific logic out of the general API. The risk is duplicated logic if business rules creep in, so it should only compose and shape.

Q40. How would you migrate a monolith? Where do you begin?

Strangler fig: put a routing facade in front, carve out a low-risk, loosely coupled capability, sync or move its data, switch the route with an easy rollback, and delete the old code. Usually first make the monolith modular internally, as that exposes the seams. Data is the hard part. Do not start with the most central entity, and don't run the old and new write paths longer than necessary.

Q41. How does distributed tracing work?

The first service creates a trace id; each hop creates a span with a parent id; the context travels in traceparent headers over HTTP and in message headers over Kafka; spans are sent asynchronously to a collector and stitched together by trace id. Sampling controls cost. Use correlation ids in logs so one id locates all logs for a request.

Q42. A request sometimes takes 8 seconds. How do you find out why?

Find a slow trace by duration and read the waterfall: which span is long, and is it self-time or waiting? Check for gaps (queueing for a thread or connection), sequential calls that could be parallel, or N+1 patterns. Correlate with metrics on saturation (pool waits, GC, DB). Since we sample at 10%, for rare cases I would temporarily raise sampling or add tail sampling that keeps slow traces.

Q43. How do you secure service-to-service calls?

Encrypt and authenticate each call: mTLS for identity and encryption, often through a mesh, plus tokens for authorisation (OAuth2 client credentials for the service's identity, and forwarding the user's JWT when acting for a user). Also restrict by network policy. Keep internal endpoints separate from public ones, and don't assume the internal network is safe.

Q44. What does the shared X-Internal-Token give you, and where does it fall short?

It keeps other processes on the network from reaching /internal/**, and it is trivial to operate. Its limits: one secret for all services, no per-service identity or least privilege, rotation requires coordination, and X-Internal-Source is only self-declared. It suits a single trusted host network and a solo operator. Moving to multiple hosts or teams would call for mTLS or client credentials.

Q45. How do you propagate user identity through async events?

Do not reuse the user's JWT, which may expire before the event is handled. Put the actor and tenant ids explicitly in the event envelope as facts, and let the consumer act as a system identity with its own authorisation. In InternalClient this is the system(...) flavour used by scheduled jobs and event handlers, as opposed to asCaller(...) inside a request.

Q46. How do you version APIs without breaking consumers?

Prefer additive, backward-compatible changes with tolerant readers. For a breaking change, add /v2 alongside /v1, migrate consumers, watch traffic per version, and retire after a stated period. Field semantics are part of the contract too. Avoid versioning every small change, and test compatibility through contract tests.

Q47. Contract tests vs end-to-end tests?

Contract tests check each consumer-provider pair in isolation, run fast in CI, and pinpoint who broke what. End-to-end tests prove the system works together but are slow and flaky and scale badly with services. Use many unit and contract tests with a small number of end-to-end happy-path tests. In a solo project with one person owning both sides, our ryfn-deploy end-to-end suite gives most of the value.

Q48. Blue-green vs canary vs rolling?

Rolling replaces instances gradually, which is cheap but mixes versions and rolls back slowly. Blue-green keeps two full environments and switches instantly, costing capacity, and is hard with long-running work. Canary exposes a small share of traffic first, judged by metrics, for the safest detection of real-world problems, but needs traffic splitting and good metrics. All of them need backward-compatible database changes.

Q49. How do you deploy a database change and code change together?

You don't deploy them atomically; you make them compatible. Expand: additive migration, old code still works. Deploy new code that writes both and reads new. Backfill. Contract: remove the old column in a later release. Every step can roll back to the previous one. Migrations run at start-up per service in our case, so concurrent instances rely on Flyway's lock.

Q50. What is the twelve-factor app? Which factor is most often broken?

A set of practices for cloud-native services: config in the environment, stateless processes, backing services as attachments, build-release-run separation, disposability, logs as streams and so on. Most often broken: stateless processes (in-memory sessions or local files) and config baked into artefacts. Our per-instance limiter is a conscious, documented exception on statelessness: it is a floor, not a guarantee.

Q51. Shared library or duplicate the code?

Share stable infrastructure with few reasons to change (security wiring, logging, error envelope); duplicate small things and anything domain-related. Sharing domain models couples release schedules. A shared library also imposes version management: consumers must rebuild, and you can run mixed versions. For the same reason, keep its dependencies small and its API backward compatible.

Q52. Tell me about the ryfn-platform trade-off.

Auto-configurations mean every service gets security, ApiResponse, outbox, tracing and OpenAPI by adding one dependency, and that made 13 services feasible for one person. The cost: a change ripples across every service, and because each executable jar embeds the platform jar, a service that is not rebuilt with mvn clean package silently keeps the old code. So after a platform change we rebuild all services. It is the same binary-coupling problem a larger team would solve with semantic versions and a compatibility window.

Q53. How do you handle data consistency between services for reporting?

Accept eventual consistency, and state how stale is acceptable. For small live reports use API composition, as our report-service does, asking owners as the caller so permissions hold. For large analytical needs, feed a warehouse or read model through CDC or events, and label data with an "as of" time. Never reach across into another service's tables.

Q54. How do you implement multi-tenancy across microservices?

Carry a verified tenant context from edge to storage: identify it from path or token, check membership, include it in internal calls, event envelopes, cache keys, logs and metrics, and put a tenant column at the front of indexes. Add fairness controls for noisy neighbours (rate limits, concurrency caps, plan limits). Test isolation specifically, because a missing org_id filter is the worst bug in the system.

Q55. What is a distributed monolith, and how do you recognise it?

Services that must change or deploy together: shared tables, a fat shared library with domain logic, synchronous chains, and "release trains". You have the operational cost of microservices with the coupling of a monolith. Measure how often a change touches several services. Fix it by merging services that always change together, or by moving ownership and decoupling with contracts.

Q56. Chatty services: how do you fix them?

First ask whether the boundary is wrong; if two services talk constantly, they may be one. Otherwise provide bulk and purpose-built endpoints, cache or replicate reference data locally, and use async where the answer is not needed at once. In our case, a run that evaluates a lookup on each row reads the table once and holds it for a minute instead of calling per row.

Q57. How do you prevent cascading failures?

Timeouts everywhere, bulkheads per dependency, circuit breakers, limited retries with jitter, load shedding at the edge, and async buffering for non-critical work. Also degrade gracefully, and make critical paths independent of non-critical ones. Our audit design is an example: recording goes through the outbox, so an audit-service outage cannot fail a business transaction.

Q58. What runs on a schedule across many instances? How do you avoid double execution?

Options: leader election (ShedLock, Kubernetes leases), or database claiming with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. We use the second in job-service: each instance polls for due jobs and claims them, and running_execution_id stops a job from running twice at once; a watchdog fails executions whose instance stopped reporting. It needs no leader, and capacity grows with instances.

Q59. What happens when an instance dies in the middle of a long job?

Work must not be tied to the process. A running job or run holds a heartbeat in the database, and a reaper notices a stale heartbeat and re-queues or fails it, which means processing must be restartable and idempotent. In run-service each worker updates heartbeat_at every 15 seconds, and the run queue re-queues (or fails) runs whose instance stopped reporting.

Q60. What would you change if RefinePoint had to scale to 100 times the load?

Measure first. Likely order: per-service instances behind Kubernetes with DNS discovery; Redis for shared rate limits; pgBouncer and read replicas; moving busy schemas such as run to their own servers; circuit breakers on critical internal calls; per-service identity in place of the shared token; versioned platform releases; then partitioning results and audit by time. The boundaries, outbox and queue-claiming designs should survive unchanged, which is the real test of the architecture.

27. Kafka & Messaging

Every senior backend interview now has a messaging block, and Kafka is the default topic. The questions are rarely "what is a topic". They are "how do you guarantee ordering", "what happens to your consumer when it rebalances in the middle of a batch", "how do you avoid sending an event when the database transaction rolls back", "what do you do with a message that always fails". This chapter builds the internal model first (log, partitions, replicas, producer pipeline, consumer group protocol), then the Spring Kafka layer you actually write code against, then the comparisons and production scenarios.

27.1 Messaging models: queue vs publish/subscribe

Two shapes cover almost every messaging system:

Point-to-point (queue) Publish/subscribe (topic)
Who gets a message Exactly one of the competing consumers Every subscriber gets its own copy
After consumption Message removed (acked and deleted) Message stays; each subscriber tracks position
Typical use Work distribution: "resize this image", "send this email" Event notification: "order placed" — billing, shipping, analytics all react
Examples RabbitMQ queue, SQS, JMS queue SNS, RabbitMQ fanout exchange, JMS topic

Kafka unifies both with one idea: the consumer group. A topic is a durable log. Consumers in the same group split the partitions between them (queue semantics: each record is processed by one member). Different groups each read the whole log independently (pub/sub semantics). Because the log is not deleted on read, a new group can be added next month and replay history.

Other vocabulary interviewers expect:

  • Message vs event vs command. A command asks one recipient to do something ("SendInvoice") and may be rejected. An event states a fact that already happened ("RunCompleted") and has any number of listeners. Events are named in the past tense; commands are imperative.
  • Push vs pull. RabbitMQ pushes to consumers (bounded by prefetch). Kafka consumers pull, which gives natural back-pressure: a slow consumer just falls behind (lag) without the broker needing to buffer for it.
  • Smart broker / dumb consumer vs dumb broker / smart consumer. RabbitMQ routes, tracks per-message acks and redelivers. Kafka just appends and serves byte ranges; consumers keep their own position (offset). That is why Kafka scales to millions of messages per second on modest hardware.

RefinePoint: we use Kafka only where an event has several independent consumers or must survive the consumer being down: rp.audit.events (every audited action, consumed by audit-service), rp.run.completed (consumed by reconciliation-service for counters and by ai-service for anomaly detection) and rp.notifications (consumed by alert-notify-service). Everything else between services is a direct REST call through InternalClient. Kafka is not a free replacement for a function call; it adds latency, operational load and eventual consistency.

27.2 Kafka architecture

  • Broker — a Kafka server process. It stores partition replicas on disk and serves produce/fetch requests.
  • Topic — a named, logical stream (orders). It is split into partitions.
  • Partition — an ordered, append-only, immutable sequence of records. It is the unit of parallelism, ordering and replication. Order is guaranteed within a partition only.
  • Offset — a 64-bit position of a record inside a partition. Offsets are per partition; offset 42 in partition 0 has nothing to do with offset 42 in partition 1.
  • Replica — a copy of a partition on a broker. One replica is the leader (all produce and, by default, all fetch requests go to it), the rest are followers that fetch from the leader exactly like consumers do. Since KIP-392, consumers may fetch from the closest follower (client.rack) to save cross-AZ traffic.
  • ISR (in-sync replicas) — the leader plus followers that have caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms (default 30 s). Only ISR members can become leader (unless unclean.leader.election.enable=true, which risks data loss).
  • Controller — the brain: assigns partitions, elects leaders, tracks broker liveness. In ZooKeeper mode one broker was elected controller through ZooKeeper; in KRaft mode a small quorum of controller nodes runs Raft over an internal __cluster_metadata log, and brokers replicate that metadata log.

High watermark and log end offset

Partition orders-0, leader on broker 1, replication factor 3

offset:     0   1   2   3   4   5   6   7
leader:    [a] [b] [c] [d] [e] [f] [g] [h]      LEO = 8
follower2: [a] [b] [c] [d] [e] [f]               LEO = 6
follower3: [a] [b] [c] [d] [e] [f] [g]           LEO = 7
                                 ^
                       High watermark = 6 (min LEO across ISR)
Consumers can read offsets 0..5 only. Records 6 and 7 are not yet "committed".

The log end offset (LEO) is the next offset a replica will write. The high watermark (HW) is the highest offset replicated to every ISR member; consumers never see records above it. That is why a record a consumer has read cannot disappear on leader failover: any new leader comes from the ISR and therefore has it.

KRaft vs ZooKeeper

ZooKeeper mode KRaft mode
Metadata store External ZooKeeper ensemble Internal Raft log __cluster_metadata
Systems to operate Two (Kafka + ZooKeeper) One
Controller failover Seconds to minutes on big clusters (reload all metadata from ZK) Near-instant (standby controllers already have the log)
Partition limit Practically ~200k per cluster Millions
Status Deprecated in 3.x, removed in Kafka 4.0 Default since 3.3 production-ready; only mode in 4.0

Storage: segments and indexes

A partition on disk is a directory of segments. Only the newest (active) segment is written; older ones are immutable and are what retention deletes or compacts.

/var/kafka-logs/orders-0/
  00000000000000000000.log        <- records, offsets 0 .. 52,113
  00000000000000000000.index      <- sparse: offset -> byte position
  00000000000000000000.timeindex  <- sparse: timestamp -> offset
  00000000000000052114.log        <- active segment (base offset 52114)
  00000000000000052114.index
  00000000000000052114.timeindex
  leader-epoch-checkpoint

A fetch for offset 60,000 picks the segment by base offset (binary search over file names), looks up the nearest earlier entry in the sparse .index (every ~4 KB, index.interval.bytes), then scans forward a few kilobytes. Segments roll at log.segment.bytes (1 GB) or log.roll.ms.

Why Kafka is fast:

  1. Sequential I/O — appends only; disks and SSDs love sequential writes.
  2. OS page cache — Kafka does not cache in the JVM heap; recently written data is read straight from the page cache, so consumers that keep up never touch the disk.
  3. Zero-copy — sendfile() (FileChannel.transferTo) moves bytes from page cache to socket without copying into user space (not possible with TLS, which must encrypt in user space).
  4. Batching and compression end to end — the producer compresses a batch, the broker stores it compressed, the consumer decompresses.
  5. Partitioning — throughput scales horizontally with partitions and brokers.

27.3 Producer internals

KafkaProducer.send() is asynchronous: it serialises, chooses a partition, appends to an in-memory batch and returns a Future. A background Sender thread groups ready batches by destination broker and ships them in one ProduceRequest per broker.

Setting Default (clients 3.x) What it does
batch.size 16384 bytes Max bytes per partition batch. Bigger = better throughput and compression
linger.ms 0 (5 from Kafka 4.0) How long to wait for a batch to fill before sending. 5–20 ms is a common throughput setting
buffer.memory 32 MB Total accumulator memory; when full, send() blocks up to max.block.ms (60 s)
compression.type none lz4/zstd usually best; snappy cheap; gzip CPU-heavy
acks all (since 3.0) How many replicas must have the record before success
retries Integer.MAX_VALUE Bounded in practice by delivery.timeout.ms (120 s)
enable.idempotence true (since 3.0) Broker de-duplicates retried batches
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection 5 Unacked requests per broker; ≤ 5 keeps order with idempotence

Partitioner and keys

  • Key present: partition = murmur2(keyBytes) % numPartitions (positive). The same key always lands in the same partition — as long as the partition count does not change.
  • Key null: since Kafka 2.4 the sticky partitioner fills one partition's batch before moving on (KIP-480); since 3.3 the built-in "uniform sticky" partitioner also avoids slow brokers (KIP-794). Older clients did round-robin per record, which produced many tiny batches.
  • Custom partitioner: implement Partitioner, e.g. to route a hot tenant to dedicated partitions.

acks: durability vs latency

acks Producer waits for Can lose data when Latency
0 Nothing (fire and forget) Any network or broker hiccup Lowest
1 Leader wrote to its log Leader dies before followers copy the record Low
all (-1) All current ISR members have it Only if ISR shrank to 1 and that broker's disk dies — prevented by min.insync.replicas=2 Higher

The durable recipe is RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all: you tolerate one broker down for writes and lose nothing on a single failure. If the ISR drops below 2, the leader rejects writes with NotEnoughReplicasException — availability is traded for durability, deliberately.

Trap: acks=all with min.insync.replicas=1 (the broker default) is barely better than acks=1: if both followers fall out of the ISR, "all" means "the leader alone".

Idempotent producer

Retries create duplicates: the broker wrote the batch but the ack was lost, so the producer sends it again. With enable.idempotence=true the broker assigns a producer id (PID) and the producer stamps each batch with a per-partition sequence number. The broker keeps the last five sequence numbers per PID/partition; a repeat is acknowledged but not written, and a gap (sequence jumped) is rejected as OutOfOrderSequenceException. This also preserves ordering with up to 5 in-flight requests, which is why the old advice "set max.in.flight to 1 for ordering" is obsolete when idempotence is on.

Scope: idempotence is per producer session and per partition. A restarted producer gets a new PID, so it does not de-duplicate an application-level resend. For that you need transactions (a stable transactional.id) or idempotent consumers.

Transactions and exactly-once

Transactions let a producer write to several partitions and commit consumer offsets atomically. This is how Kafka gives exactly-once for read-process-write within Kafka (consume from topic A, produce to topic B).

  • transactional.id is stable across restarts; on initTransactions() the coordinator bumps the epoch and fences any zombie instance still using the old epoch (ProducerFencedException).
  • Consumers with isolation.level=read_committed read only up to the last stable offset (LSO) and skip aborted records. Default is read_uncommitted.
  • Exactly-once ends at the Kafka boundary. If your processing writes to PostgreSQL or calls Paddle, a Kafka transaction cannot roll that back. For external side effects you need idempotence (dedupe table, idempotency keys) — "effectively once".

27.4 Consumer internals

The poll loop

try (var consumer = new KafkaConsumer<String, String>(props)) {
    consumer.subscribe(List.of("rp.run.completed"));
    while (running) {
        ConsumerRecords<String, String> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
        for (var r : records) handle(r);          // must finish within max.poll.interval.ms for the whole batch
        consumer.commitSync();                    // at-least-once: commit after processing
    }
}

KafkaConsumer is not thread-safe; one consumer per thread. Liveness has two separate checks:

Setting Default Detects
heartbeat.interval.ms 3 s Background heartbeat thread pings the group coordinator
session.timeout.ms 45 s (since 3.0) Process dead / network partition — no heartbeats
max.poll.interval.ms 5 min Process alive but stuck — no poll() call in time; member leaves the group
max.poll.records 500 Records returned per poll — lower it if processing is slow

Consumer groups and partition assignment

One broker is the group coordinator for each group (chosen by hashing group.id onto a partition of __consumer_offsets). In the classic protocol, members send JoinGroup; one member is elected leader and computes the assignment client-side using the configured assignor; the coordinator distributes it via SyncGroup.

Assignor Behaviour
RangeAssignor Per topic, contiguous ranges; co-partitions topics with the same count (useful for joins), can be uneven
RoundRobinAssignor Spreads all partitions evenly; everything moves on rebalance
StickyAssignor Balanced and keeps previous assignments, but still eager (stop-the-world)
CooperativeStickyAssignor Sticky and incremental: only the partitions that move are revoked

Rules: a partition is consumed by at most one member of a group; members beyond the partition count sit idle. Four partitions and six consumers means two idle consumers.

Rebalancing: eager vs cooperative

Eager rebalancing stops the whole group ("stop the world") on every membership change — painful with 50 consumers and a rolling deploy. Cooperative sticky does two short rounds and only pauses the partitions that move. Other tools:

  • Static membership (group.instance.id): a restarted pod with the same id rejoins within session.timeout.ms without triggering a rebalance. Great for Kubernetes StatefulSets and rolling restarts.
  • KIP-848 next-generation protocol (group.protocol=consumer, GA in Kafka 4.0): the broker computes assignments incrementally; no global synchronisation barrier, much faster rebalances.
  • ConsumerRebalanceListener.onPartitionsRevoked is where you commit offsets for in-flight work before losing a partition; Spring Kafka does this for you.

Offset commits and delivery semantics

Committed offsets live in the compacted internal topic __consumer_offsets, keyed by (group, topic, partition). The committed value is the next offset to read (last processed + 1).

Strategy How Semantics
Auto commit enable.auto.commit=true, every auto.commit.interval.ms (5 s) during poll() At-least-once in practice (commit happens on a later poll), but can be at-most-once if you hand records to other threads
Commit before processing commitSync() then process At-most-once — crash after commit loses the message
Commit after processing process then commitSync()/commitAsync() At-least-once — crash before commit redelivers
Transactional sendOffsetsToTransaction Exactly-once for Kafka-to-Kafka
Offsets stored with the result Save offset in the same DB transaction as the business change, seek() on assignment Exactly-once into that DB

auto.offset.reset decides what happens when the group has no committed offset (new group, or offset expired after offsets.retention.minutes, 7 days): latest (default — start at the end, skip history) or earliest (read from the beginning).

RefinePoint: alert-notify-service reads rp.notifications twice. The service's normal consumer group stores each notification once (instances share partitions). A second listener uses a group of its own per instance with auto.offset.reset=latest, so every instance hears every notification from now on and pushes it to the browser pages whose live stream it holds. Same topic, both semantics, chosen purely by group id.

27.5 Ordering guarantees

Kafka guarantees order per partition, for records written by one producer. To keep the events of one entity in order, give them the same key (runId, orderId, orgId), so they hash to the same partition, and keep that partition's consumer single-threaded for that key.

Ordering breaks when:

  1. Records for one entity have different keys or null keys.
  2. Partition count is increased — hash % n changes, new events for an old key go to a different partition while old ones may be unconsumed.
  3. Retries without idempotence and max.in.flight > 1 — batch 1 fails, batch 2 succeeds, batch 1's retry lands after it.
  4. The consumer hands records to a thread pool, or uses non-blocking retry topics (a failed record is moved aside while later records proceed).
  5. The producer side sends from several threads/instances without coordinating per key.

RefinePoint: the OutboxRelay sends outbox rows to Kafka in seq order with the row's event_key as the Kafka key. It waits for each send (kafka.send(...).get(10, SECONDS)) and, if one fails, records attempts/last_error and stops the batch — it does not skip ahead to row 101 while row 100 is unsent. The next tick (every second) retries from the oldest unsent row. Several instances can run the relay because rows are claimed with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED.

27.6 Retention and log compaction

Policy cleanup.policy What remains Use for
Delete (default) delete Records younger than retention.ms (7 days) and/or within retention.bytes per partition Event streams, logs, metrics
Compact compact At least the latest value per key Changelogs, current state (user profile, config, __consumer_offsets)
Both compact,delete Latest per key, but also dropped after retention Bounded state

Retention deletes whole closed segments, never individual records, so data can live slightly longer than retention.ms (until its segment rolls and ages out).

Compaction runs in background log cleaner threads over the inactive "dirty" part of the log once min.cleanable.dirty.ratio (0.5) is reached. A record with a key and a null value is a tombstone: it deletes the key, and the tombstone itself is removed after delete.retention.ms (1 day) — consumers must read the compacted topic within that window or miss the delete.

Before compaction:  k1=A  k2=B  k1=C  k3=D  k2=null  k1=E
After compaction:   k3=D  k2=null  k1=E      (offsets preserved, gaps allowed)

27.7 Consumer lag and monitoring

Lag = log end offset − committed offset, per partition. It is the single most important consumer metric: it tells you whether consumers keep up and how stale downstream data is.

kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --describe --group audit-service
# GROUP          TOPIC             PARTITION  CURRENT-OFFSET  LOG-END-OFFSET  LAG   CONSUMER-ID
# audit-service  rp.audit.events   0          184211          184213          2     consumer-1-...
# audit-service  rp.audit.events   1          90112           131900          41788 consumer-2-...

What to watch:

  • Consumer: lag per partition and lag in time (Burrow, Kafka Lag Exporter, or records-lag-max from the client's JMX), rebalance rate, commit failures, processing time per record.
  • Producer: record-error-rate, request-latency-avg, batch-size-avg, compression-rate-avg, buffer-available-bytes (near zero = send() will block).
  • Broker: under-replicated partitions (should be 0), offline partitions, ISR shrink/expand rate, request handler idle %, disk usage, network throughput.

Lag on one partition only is a hot key or a stuck consumer; lag on all partitions is a throughput problem (slow downstream, too few consumers, too few partitions). Spring Boot exposes the client metrics through Micrometer automatically (kafka.consumer.fetch.manager.records.lag.max).

27.8 Errors, poison messages and dead-letter topics

A poison message is one that will fail every time: bad JSON, an unknown schema version, a business rule that can never pass. With naive at-least-once code, the consumer fails, does not commit, re-polls the same record and loops forever while lag grows on that partition.

Classify failures first:

Failure Example Treatment
Deserialization Malformed JSON, wrong Avro schema ErrorHandlingDeserializer → straight to DLT, no retry
Permanent business Validation fails, referenced entity missing forever No retry (mark not retryable) → DLT
Transient DB timeout, HTTP 503 from a dependency Retry with backoff, then DLT

Blocking retries: DefaultErrorHandler

Spring Kafka's DefaultErrorHandler (replaced SeekToCurrentErrorHandler in 2.8) re-seeks the partition to the failed record and redelivers it in the same consumer thread. Default back-off is FixedBackOff(0, 9) — 10 attempts in total. After that the recoverer runs.

@Bean
DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) {
    var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template,
        (rec, ex) -> new TopicPartition(rec.topic() + ".DLT", rec.partition()));   // default naming
    var backOff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(4);
    backOff.setInitialInterval(500); backOff.setMultiplier(2.0); backOff.setMaxInterval(5_000);
    var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backOff);
    handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(ValidationException.class, JsonProcessingException.class);
    return handler;
}

The DLT record carries headers like kafka_dlt-exception-message, kafka_dlt-exception-stacktrace, kafka_dlt-original-topic, -partition, -offset. Blocking retries keep order but block the partition while retrying, so total back-off must stay well under max.poll.interval.ms.

Non-blocking retries: @RetryableTopic

@RetryableTopic(attempts = "4", backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2.0),
                exclude = ValidationException.class, dltStrategy = DltStrategy.FAIL_ON_ERROR)
@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "fulfilment")
void onOrder(OrderPlaced e) { fulfilment.handle(e); }

@DltHandler
void dlt(OrderPlaced e, @Header(KafkaHeaders.RECEIVED_TOPIC) String topic) { alerts.parked(e, topic); }

The failed record is republished to a retry topic with a due timestamp; the retry consumer pauses its partition until the delay has elapsed. The main partition keeps flowing — but ordering for that key is lost, because later records for the same key proceed while the earlier one waits. Use blocking retries for ordered streams (balances, state changes), non-blocking for independent messages (emails, thumbnails).

RefinePoint: our listeners parse every message through ConsumedEvents.parse(), which returns null and logs an error for anything that is not a valid EventEnvelope, so one bad message cannot block a topic. Real failures (database down) throw and are redelivered, and idempotency makes the redelivery harmless.

27.9 Spring Kafka in practice

spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: ${KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP}
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      acks: all
      properties:
        enable.idempotence: true
        linger.ms: 10
        compression.type: lz4
    consumer:
      group-id: audit-service
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      max-poll-records: 200
      key-deserializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
        partition.assignment.strategy: org.apache.kafka.clients.consumer.CooperativeStickyAssignor
    listener:
      ack-mode: record          # or batch (default), manual, manual_immediate
      concurrency: 3            # 3 consumer threads per instance
    security:
      protocol: SSL
  • KafkaTemplate wraps the producer. In Spring Kafka 3.x send() returns CompletableFuture<SendResult<K,V>> (2.x returned ListenableFuture). Calling .get() makes it synchronous; whenComplete keeps it async.
  • @KafkaListener is backed by a ConcurrentMessageListenerContainer; concurrency = n creates n KafkaMessageListenerContainers, each with its own KafkaConsumer and thread. Effective parallelism = min(total threads across instances, partitions).
  • Spring sets enable.auto.commit=false and the container commits for you according to AckMode: BATCH (default — after all records from a poll are processed), RECORD (after each), TIME/COUNT, MANUAL (you call Acknowledgment.acknowledge(), committed with the next batch), MANUAL_IMMEDIATE (commit now).
  • Batch listener: List<ConsumerRecord<K,V>> parameter with batchListener=true; good for bulk inserts. On failure throw BatchListenerFailedException(index) so the handler knows which record failed and commits the ones before it.
  • Observation: template.setObservationEnabled(true) and containerProperties.setObservationEnabled(true) propagate tracing headers (traceparent) through Kafka.
@KafkaListener(topics = "#{@topics.runCompleted()}", concurrency = "2")
public void onRunCompleted(String message, Acknowledgment ack) {
    EventEnvelope env = consumed.parse(message);
    if (env != null) tx.executeWithoutResult(s -> {
        if (consumed.firstTime("run-counter", env.id())) counters.apply(consumed.payload(env, RunCompletedEvent.class));
    });
    ack.acknowledge();   // MANUAL ack mode
}

RefinePoint: the topic name in @KafkaListener is a SpEL call on a bean (#{@topics.runCompleted()}), because TopicNames adds an environment prefix (nonprod.). The local stack uses the dev server's topics with consumer groups prefixed local., so each environment gets every event — a neat demonstration that groups, not topics, decide who sees what.

27.10 Schema evolution and envelopes

Producers and consumers are deployed independently, so the message format is a contract that must evolve without breaking either side.

Format Schema Size Evolution
JSON Implicit (or JSON Schema) Large Tolerant readers: ignore unknown fields, default missing ones
Avro + Schema Registry Required, stored in registry; message carries a 5-byte header (magic byte + schema id) Compact Registry enforces compatibility on register
Protobuf .proto, field numbers Compact Never reuse field numbers; add optional fields

Schema Registry compatibility modes:

Mode Guarantee Allowed change Deploy order
BACKWARD (default) New schema can read old data Delete fields, add fields with defaults Consumers first
FORWARD Old schema can read new data Add fields, delete fields with defaults Producers first
FULL Both Add/delete only fields with defaults Any order
*_TRANSITIVE Against all previous versions, not just the last Same —

Subject naming: TopicNameStrategy (one schema per topic, default) or RecordNameStrategy/TopicRecordNameStrategy (several event types on one topic).
