RefinePoint: we use a JSON envelope — record EventEnvelope(String id, String type, String source, Instant occurredAt, JsonNode payload). id is a UUID that consumers use to ignore redeliveries; type lets several event types share a topic; source names the producing service; payload stays a JsonNode until the consumer converts it to its own record with consumed.payload(envelope, RunCompletedEvent.class). Consumers are tolerant readers (Jackson configured to ignore unknown properties), so adding a payload field never breaks an older consumer. With a single team and three topics, a registry would be overhead; with many teams it becomes essential.

27.11 Idempotent consumers

At-least-once delivery means every consumer must tolerate duplicates. Duplicates come from producer retries without idempotence, outbox relays that crash after sending but before marking sent, consumer crashes before commit, and rebalances that revoke a partition mid-batch.

Techniques, from strongest:

  1. Dedupe table in the same transaction as the side effect: INSERT INTO consumed_events(consumer, event_id) ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING; if 0 rows inserted, skip.
  2. Naturally idempotent operations: UPDATE run SET status='COMPLETED' WHERE id=?, upserts, set semantics.
  3. Version/sequence checks: apply only if event.version > row.version.
  4. Idempotency keys passed to external APIs (payment providers dedupe on them).
@Transactional
public void handle(EventEnvelope env) {
    if (!consumed.firstTime("audit-writer", env.id())) return;   // INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING == 0 rows
    auditRepository.save(AuditEntry.from(consumed.payload(env, AuditEvent.class)));
}

The insert and the business write commit or roll back together. If the business write fails, the dedupe row rolls back too and the redelivery is processed properly.

RefinePoint: OutboxRelay.purge() runs hourly: sent outbox rows are deleted after 7 days, consumed_events rows after 30 days. The dedupe window must be longer than any realistic redelivery delay (consumer outage + retention), otherwise a very late duplicate would be processed again.

27.12 Kafka Streams basics

Kafka Streams is a library (not a cluster) for stateful stream processing inside your JVM. Scaling = run more instances; partitions are divided between them like a consumer group.

  • KStream — a stream of independent events (every record is a fact).
  • KTable — a changelog viewed as a table (latest value per key), partitioned.
  • GlobalKTable — a full copy on every instance (small reference data, joins without co-partitioning).
  • State stores — local RocksDB, backed by a compacted changelog topic so state is restored after failure. Standby replicas keep warm copies.
  • Stateless ops: filter, map, flatMap; stateful: groupByKey().count(), aggregate, windowed aggregations (tumbling, hopping, sliding, session), joins (stream-stream windowed, stream-table, table-table).
  • processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 wraps consume-process-produce and state changelog writes in transactions.
builder.stream("payments", Consumed.with(Serdes.String(), paymentSerde))
       .groupByKey()
       .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeWithNoGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(5)))
       .count(Materialized.as("payments-per-account-5m"))
       .toStream()
       .filter((windowedKey, count) -> count > 20)
       .to("suspicious-accounts");

27.13 Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS/SNS

Kafka RabbitMQ SQS / SNS
Model Distributed commit log Broker with exchanges → queues Managed queue (SQS) + managed pub/sub (SNS)
Routing By topic + key → partition Exchanges: direct, topic (wildcards), fanout, headers; bindings SNS topic → subscriptions with filter policies → SQS/Lambda/HTTP
Consumption Pull, consumer tracks offset Push with prefetch (basic.qos), per-message ack/nack/requeue Pull (long polling up to 20 s), visibility timeout, delete to ack
After read Kept until retention Deleted on ack Deleted on DeleteMessage
Replay Yes (seek to offset/time) No (except RabbitMQ Streams) No (SNS archive/replay for FIFO only)
Ordering Per partition Per queue with one consumer Standard: best-effort. FIFO: per message group id
Delivery At-least-once; exactly-once within Kafka At-least-once with publisher confirms + manual acks Standard at-least-once; FIFO exactly-once processing with 5-min dedup id
Dead letters Application pattern (DLT) Dead-letter exchange (DLX), TTL Redrive policy, maxReceiveCount
Throughput Very high (millions/s) High (tens of thousands/s per queue) Practically unlimited (standard); FIFO limited per group
Ops Heavy unless managed (MSK, Confluent, Aiven) Moderate None
Best for Event streaming, event sourcing, CDC, many consumers, replay Task queues, complex routing, RPC, per-message priority/TTL AWS-native decoupling without running a broker

RabbitMQ reliability vocabulary: publisher confirms (broker acks the publish), mandatory flag (return unroutable messages), durable queues + persistent messages, quorum queues (Raft-replicated; the modern replacement for classic mirrored queues), manual consumer acks and prefetch to bound in-flight messages per consumer.

27.14 Sizing partitions and tuning

Partition count — estimate from target throughput: partitions ≥ max(T / Tp, T / Tc) where T is the target throughput, Tp what one producer can push to one partition, Tc what one consumer thread can process. If a consumer handles 500 records/s and you need 10,000/s at peak, you need at least 20 partitions (and 20 consumer threads). Add head-room for growth because increasing partitions later breaks key→partition mapping.

Costs of too many partitions: more open file handles, longer leader elections and controller work, more memory in producers (one batch per partition), slower rebalances, and end-to-end latency for replication. Hundreds per broker are fine; tens of thousands need care (KRaft raised the ceiling).

Goal Producer Consumer Broker/topic
Throughput linger.ms 10–50, batch.size 64–256 KB, compression.type=lz4/zstd fetch.min.bytes ↑, max.poll.records ↑, batch listeners, more partitions More partitions, more brokers, fast disks
Latency linger.ms=0, acks=1 (if loss acceptable) fetch.max.wait.ms ↓ Fewer replicas in the critical path, same-AZ clients
Durability acks=all, idempotence Commit after processing RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, unclean.leader.election.enable=false

Message size: default max ~1 MB (message.max.bytes, max.request.size). For large payloads use the claim-check pattern: store the file in S3/blob storage and send a reference.

RefinePoint: a reconciliation run can produce hundreds of thousands of result rows. We never put them on Kafka — rp.run.completed carries the run id, counts and status (a small JSON envelope), and consumers fetch details through the service API if they need them. That is claim-check by design.

27.15 Real production scenarios

Scenario 1 — "Lag keeps growing on one partition." One hot key (a big tenant) or one stuck record. Check kafka-consumer-groups --describe, find the partition, look at the committed offset that is not moving, dump that record (kafka-console-consumer --partition 3 --offset 81234 --max-messages 1). If it is a poison message, the error handler should DLT it; if it is a hot key, consider a composite key (tenant + entity) to spread load while keeping per-entity order.

Scenario 2 — "Consumers keep rebalancing every few minutes." Processing a poll's worth of records takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms, so the member is kicked out, its partitions move, and the same slow batch hits the next member. Fix: lower max.poll.records, speed up processing, raise max.poll.interval.ms, use cooperative sticky + static membership.

Scenario 3 — "We published the event but the DB transaction rolled back" (or the reverse: DB committed, Kafka send failed). This is the dual-write problem. Fix: transactional outbox (write the event into the same DB transaction, relay later) or CDC with Debezium reading the WAL.

Scenario 4 — "After a deploy, consumers re-processed a week of data." The group id changed (or offsets expired after 7 days without commits) and auto.offset.reset=earliest. Pin group ids in configuration, never derive them from hostnames for shared-work groups, and make consumers idempotent anyway.

Scenario 5 — "Producer send() blocks for 60 seconds." The accumulator is full (buffer.memory) because brokers are unreachable or slow; max.block.ms expires with TimeoutException. In a request thread this stalls the API — another reason to write to an outbox table and relay asynchronously.

27.16 Interview questions and answers

Q1. What is Kafka, in one sentence, and why not just use a database table as a queue?

Kafka is a distributed, partitioned, replicated append-only log that many independent consumer groups read at their own pace. A table works as a queue for modest volumes with one kind of consumer (we do exactly that for run and job queues with SKIP LOCKED), but it does not give you cheap fan-out to many consumers, replay from any point, millions of messages per second, or retention without bloating the OLTP database. Choose a table when the work and its state belong to one service; choose Kafka when many services react to the same facts.

Q2. Queue vs publish/subscribe — how does Kafka support both?

Through consumer groups. Members of one group share the partitions, so each record is processed once per group (queue). Each group gets every record (pub/sub). Adding a new subscriber is just a new group.id; the producer does not change.

Q3. What is a partition and why does it matter so much?

A partition is an ordered, append-only log stored on one leader broker and replicated to followers. It is the unit of ordering (order is only per partition), parallelism (at most one consumer per group per partition) and replication. Picking the key and partition count is the main design decision for any topic.

Q4. Explain leader, follower, ISR and high watermark.

Each partition has one leader that handles reads and writes, and followers that fetch from it. The ISR is the set of replicas caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms. The high watermark is the highest offset copied to every ISR member; consumers read only up to it, so a record visible to consumers survives a leader failover because the new leader is elected from the ISR.

Q5. What happens when a broker that leads several partitions dies?

The controller notices (missed heartbeats in KRaft, ZooKeeper session expiry in the old mode), picks a new leader for each affected partition from its ISR, bumps the leader epoch, and publishes new metadata. Producers and consumers get NOT_LEADER_OR_FOLLOWER errors, refresh metadata and reconnect to the new leaders; with retries enabled this is transparent apart from a latency spike. When the broker returns, it truncates its log to the leader-epoch boundary, catches up, rejoins the ISR, and preferred-leader election eventually moves leadership back.

Q6. What is unclean leader election?

Electing a replica that is not in the ISR when no ISR member is available. The partition becomes available again but records that only the old leader had are lost and offsets may be reused. Default is false: prefer unavailability over silent data loss. Some log/metrics topics enable it to favour availability.

Q7. KRaft vs ZooKeeper — what changed and why?

KRaft moves cluster metadata into an internal Raft-replicated log managed by controller nodes, removing ZooKeeper. Benefits: one system to run, faster controller failover (standbys already hold the metadata), and support for millions of partitions. ZooKeeper mode was deprecated in 3.x and removed in Kafka 4.0, so new clusters are KRaft-only; migration from ZK uses a bridge mode in 3.x.

Q8. Why is Kafka fast even though it writes to disk?

Sequential appends, heavy use of the OS page cache instead of a JVM heap cache, zero-copy sendfile from page cache to socket, batching and compression end to end, and horizontal scaling through partitions. Consumers that keep up read from memory, not disk.

Q9. What is a log segment and why does Kafka use them?

A partition is split into segment files (default 1 GB or log.roll.ms), each with a sparse offset index and a time index. Only the active segment is written. Segments make retention cheap (delete a whole file), make compaction incremental, and keep index lookups fast (binary search on base offsets, then a small scan).

Q10. Walk me through what happens inside producer.send().

Interceptors run, the key and value are serialised, the partitioner chooses a partition (murmur2 hash of the key, or sticky for null keys), and the record is appended to that partition's current batch in the RecordAccumulator. send() returns a future immediately. The Sender thread drains batches that are full (batch.size) or old enough (linger.ms), groups them by leader broker, and sends one produce request per broker. When the broker acknowledges according to acks, the futures and callbacks complete; retriable errors are retried until delivery.timeout.ms.

Q11. What do linger.ms and batch.size trade off?

Latency for throughput. linger.ms=0 sends as soon as the Sender is free (small batches, more requests); a few milliseconds of linger lets batches fill, improves compression ratio and cuts request count. Under heavy load batches fill anyway, so linger costs nothing; under light load it adds up to linger.ms of latency per record. Kafka 4.0 changed the default linger to 5 ms for this reason.

Q12. Explain acks 0, 1 and all.

0: the producer does not wait — fastest, may lose data silently. 1: the leader has written it — lost if the leader dies before followers copy it. all: every in-sync replica has it — combined with min.insync.replicas=2 and RF=3, no acknowledged record is lost on a single broker failure. acks=all and idempotence are the defaults since Kafka 3.0.

Q13. What is min.insync.replicas and what happens when it is not met?

The minimum ISR size for a write with acks=all to succeed. If the ISR shrinks below it, produce requests fail with NotEnoughReplicas (the topic stays readable). It is a durability floor: you choose to stop accepting writes rather than accept writes that exist on only one disk.

Q14. How does the idempotent producer work, and what does it not cover?

The broker gives the producer a producer id; the producer numbers each batch per partition. The broker drops a batch whose sequence it has already written (a retry after a lost ack) and rejects out-of-order sequences, so retries cannot create duplicates or reorder records, even with five requests in flight. It does not cover a restarted producer (new id), an application that calls send() twice for the same business event, or duplicates created downstream — those need transactions or idempotent consumers.

Q15. Explain Kafka transactions and exactly-once semantics.

A transactional producer (stable transactional.id) registers partitions with a transaction coordinator, writes records, adds the consumer's offsets with sendOffsetsToTransaction, then commits; the coordinator writes commit markers to every involved partition. read_committed consumers only see committed data (up to the last stable offset). The epoch on transactional.id fences zombie instances. The result is exactly-once for consume-transform-produce entirely inside Kafka. It is not exactly-once for side effects in other systems.

Q16. Can you get exactly-once from Kafka into PostgreSQL?

Not with Kafka transactions alone; the database is outside them. Two practical options: (1) idempotent processing — a dedupe table or upsert in the same DB transaction as the business change, so redeliveries do nothing (what we do); (2) store the consumed offset in the same DB transaction and on partition assignment seek() to the stored offset instead of using Kafka's committed offset. Both give effectively-once results.

Q17. What is the dual-write problem, and how does the transactional outbox solve it?

Writing to the database and to Kafka are two separate systems with no shared transaction, so one can succeed and the other fail: an event for a rolled-back order, or a committed order with no event. The outbox writes the event as a row in the same DB transaction as the business change; a relay (polling or CDC like Debezium) publishes rows to Kafka afterwards and marks them sent. If the transaction rolls back, the event never existed; if Kafka is down, events wait in the table. Delivery becomes at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

RefinePoint: EventPublisher.publish(topic, key, type, payload) builds an EventEnvelope with a fresh UUID and inserts it into outbox_events inside the caller's transaction. OutboxRelay sends rows every second in seq order. When Kafka was unreachable during a cluster maintenance window, nothing failed for users; audit entries and run counters simply caught up afterwards.

Q18. Polling outbox vs CDC (Debezium) — trade-offs?

Polling: simple, no extra infrastructure, a little DB load and up to one poll interval of latency; ordering and locking are your code. CDC: reads the WAL, near real-time, no polling queries, but needs Kafka Connect, Debezium, replication slots and their monitoring (a stuck slot makes the WAL grow until the disk fills). For a small team, polling with SKIP LOCKED is the pragmatic choice; at high event rates CDC wins.

Q19. How does a consumer group assign partitions?

Members join through the group coordinator; in the classic protocol one member (the group leader) runs the assignor and the coordinator distributes the result. Range assigns contiguous ranges per topic, round robin spreads evenly, sticky keeps prior assignments, cooperative sticky also moves partitions incrementally. In the KIP-848 protocol the broker computes the assignment itself.

Q20. What triggers a rebalance?

A member joining or leaving (deploy, scale out, crash), a member exceeding session.timeout.ms without heartbeats, a member exceeding max.poll.interval.ms between polls, subscription changes, or partition count changes on subscribed topics (including new topics matching a regex subscription).

Q21. Eager vs cooperative rebalancing?

Eager: every member revokes all partitions, everyone rejoins, a new assignment is handed out — the whole group stops. Cooperative (incremental): members keep partitions that are not moving and only revoke the ones being reassigned, over two quick rounds; processing continues on unaffected partitions. Use CooperativeStickyAssignor (and in Kafka 4.0, the new consumer protocol) for large groups and frequent deploys.

Q22. What is static group membership?

Setting group.instance.id per consumer instance makes membership survive restarts: a member that leaves and returns with the same id within session.timeout.ms gets its old partitions back without a rebalance. It removes rebalance storms during rolling restarts; the trade-off is that a truly dead member is only detected after the session timeout.

Q23. Difference between session.timeout.ms and max.poll.interval.ms?

Session timeout detects a dead process: the background heartbeat thread stopped. Max poll interval detects a live but stuck process: the application thread did not call poll() in time. A consumer doing a 10-minute operation per poll keeps heartbeating but is still evicted after 5 minutes by the poll interval.

Q24. Your consumer processes a batch slowly and keeps getting CommitFailedException. Why?

Processing the batch took longer than max.poll.interval.ms, so the consumer was removed from the group and its partitions given to another member; when it tries to commit, the generation is stale and the commit is rejected. The records will be reprocessed by the new owner. Fix: reduce max.poll.records, make processing faster or asynchronous with pause/resume, or increase the interval, and make processing idempotent.

Q25. Auto commit vs manual commit?

Auto commit commits the offsets returned by the previous poll every 5 seconds during poll(). It is at-least-once if you process synchronously in the poll loop, but if you hand records to another thread it can commit before processing (at-most-once). Manual commit after processing gives explicit at-least-once. Spring Kafka disables auto commit and commits from the container according to AckMode, which is what you want in almost all cases.

Q26. commitSync vs commitAsync?

commitSync blocks and retries until success or a non-retriable error; commitAsync does not block or retry (a retried older commit could overwrite a newer one). Common pattern: commitAsync in the loop for speed, commitSync on shutdown and in onPartitionsRevoked.

Q27. Explain at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once with Kafka.

At-most-once: commit before processing; a crash loses the message. At-least-once: process then commit; a crash causes redelivery, so duplicates are possible. Exactly-once: Kafka transactions for Kafka-to-Kafka pipelines, or idempotent/offset-in-DB processing for external sinks. In practice: at-least-once plus idempotent consumers is the standard answer.

Q28. What does auto.offset.reset do, and what is the classic incident?

It applies only when the group has no valid committed offset: latest starts from the end, earliest from the beginning, none throws. Incident: a group id is renamed or offsets expire after seven days of inactivity, and with earliest the service reprocesses the whole retained topic (duplicate emails), or with latest silently skips everything produced while it was down.

Q29. How does Kafka guarantee ordering, and how do you keep events of one order in sequence?

Only within a partition. Use the order id as the key so all its events go to one partition; keep idempotence on so retries do not reorder; process each partition sequentially on the consumer (no unordered thread pool, no non-blocking retry topics for that stream); and do not change the partition count casually.

Q30. What happens to key ordering if you add partitions to a topic?

hash(key) % n changes, so new records for an existing key may go to a different partition than its older records. If consumers of the new partition run ahead of the old one, events for that key are processed out of order. Kafka does not move existing data. Options: over-provision partitions from day one, create a new topic with more partitions and migrate consumers at a quiet point, or tolerate reordering with version checks in consumers.

Q31. How do you process a partition in parallel without losing per-key order?

Inside one consumer, dispatch records to N worker queues by hash(key) % N; each queue is processed by one thread, so per-key order holds. Commit an offset only when every record below it is done (track the lowest incomplete offset per partition). Confluent's Parallel Consumer library implements exactly this with key-level ordering.

Q32. How does RefinePoint keep event order from the outbox?

The relay reads the oldest unsent rows ordered by seq, locks them with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, sends each one synchronously with its event key, marks it sent, and on the first failure records the error and stops the batch. A failed event is never overtaken by a later one, and keys put related events on the same partition. Note the caveat: with two relay instances, each claims a different batch, so global order across batches is not strict — per-key order holds in practice because a key's events are written in order and claimed oldest first. If strict global order mattered we would run one relay with a database advisory lock.

Q33. What is log compaction and when do you use it?

A cleanup policy that keeps at least the latest record for every key and removes older ones, with null-value tombstones deleting a key. Use it for topics that represent current state — configuration, entity snapshots, KTable changelogs, __consumer_offsets — so a new consumer can rebuild state by reading the topic from the start without replaying all history.

Q34. Does retention delete records exactly after retention.ms?

No. Retention deletes whole inactive segments whose newest record is older than the limit. A record in the active segment, or in a segment with newer records, stays until that segment rolls and ages out. Also, retention is independent of consumption: unread records are deleted too, and a consumer that falls more than the retention period behind gets OffsetOutOfRange and resets per auto.offset.reset.

Q35. What is consumer lag and how do you alert on it?

The difference between the log end offset and the committed offset per partition. Alert on lag in time (how old is the oldest unprocessed record) rather than raw count, and on a lag that keeps increasing for N minutes. Tools: kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe, Burrow, Kafka Lag Exporter, Micrometer records-lag-max into Prometheus and Grafana.

Q36. How do you handle a poison message?

Stop it from blocking the partition: deserialise with ErrorHandlingDeserializer so bad bytes become an error rather than an infinite loop, classify exceptions into retryable and non-retryable, retry transient failures with bounded back-off, and send the rest to a dead-letter topic with diagnostic headers. Alert on DLT growth, and build a replay tool that re-publishes fixed messages to the original topic.

Q37. DefaultErrorHandler vs @RetryableTopic?

DefaultErrorHandler retries in place by seeking back to the failed record: ordering is preserved but the partition is blocked during back-off, and long back-off risks exceeding max.poll.interval.ms. @RetryableTopic moves the failed record to delayed retry topics and finally a DLT: the main partition keeps flowing but per-key ordering is lost and you get extra topics to operate. Ordered state changes → blocking; independent tasks like emails → non-blocking.

Q38. What does DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer do exactly?

After retries are exhausted it publishes the failed record, with the original key, value and headers plus exception headers (message, stack trace, original topic, partition, offset, timestamp), to <topic>.DLT by default, on the same partition number, using a KafkaTemplate. The DLT therefore needs at least as many partitions as the source, or you supply a destination resolver. After publishing successfully the error handler commits the original offset so consumption continues.

Q39. How do you write an idempotent consumer?

Give every event a unique id at creation, and in the consumer record that id in a dedupe table in the same transaction as the side effect; if the insert affects zero rows, skip. Alternatively make the operation naturally idempotent (upsert, set status) or check entity versions. Clean the dedupe table after a window longer than any possible redelivery.

Q40. Why is the dedupe insert in the same transaction as the business change, not before it?

If you insert the event id first and commit, then the business change fails, the redelivery is skipped forever — the event is lost. If both are in one transaction, either both are committed (duplicate later skipped) or neither (redelivery processes it properly).

Q41. What is in your event envelope and why?

A unique id (dedupe), a type (routing and versioning several events on one topic), a source service (debugging), an occurred-at timestamp (ordering checks, lag in time), and the payload. Tracing context travels in Kafka headers rather than the body. In RefinePoint it is the EventEnvelope record with the payload as JsonNode so each consumer maps it to its own class.

Q42. Explain Schema Registry compatibility modes.

BACKWARD: consumers on the new schema can read data written with the old one — add fields with defaults or remove fields; upgrade consumers first. FORWARD: old consumers can read new data — upgrade producers first. FULL: both. The _TRANSITIVE variants check against all historical versions, which matters when a topic retains months of data. The registry rejects an incompatible schema at registration, which catches the mistake in CI instead of in production.

Q43. How do you evolve a JSON event without a registry?

Treat the schema as additive: only add optional fields, never rename or change types, never reuse a field name with a new meaning. Consumers ignore unknown properties and default missing ones. For a breaking change, publish a new event type or version (RunCompleted.v2) side by side, migrate consumers, then stop the old one. Keep contract tests between producer and consumer.

Q44. How many partitions should a topic have?

Enough for peak consumer parallelism and throughput, with head-room: partitions ≥ peak messages per second divided by what one consumer thread can process. A low-volume internal topic: 3–6 is fine. A high-volume topic: dozens. Avoid thousands per topic without reason — more partitions cost memory, file handles, rebalance and failover time. Decide up front, because increasing later breaks key placement.

Q45. You have 6 partitions and scale your service to 10 instances with concurrency 1. What happens?

Six consumers get one partition each and four sit idle; they only help as hot standbys during rebalances. To use 10 consumers you need at least 10 partitions. With Spring concurrency=3 on 2 instances you have 6 threads — a good match for 6 partitions.

Q46. How does concurrency work in Spring Kafka?

ConcurrentMessageListenerContainer creates concurrency child containers, each with its own KafkaConsumer and thread in the same group. Partitions are spread across all threads of all instances. Concurrency above the partition count just creates idle consumers.

Q47. What are the Spring Kafka AckMode options?

RECORD (commit after each record), BATCH (default, after all records of a poll), TIME and COUNT (periodic), COUNT_TIME, MANUAL (listener calls acknowledge(); queued and committed with the batch), MANUAL_IMMEDIATE (commit synchronously on acknowledge()). Manual modes require an Acknowledgment parameter. nack(Duration) re-seeks and redelivers after a sleep.

Q48. When would you use a batch listener?

When per-record overhead dominates: bulk inserts into the database (JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate), writing to a search index, calling an API that accepts batches. Partial failures need care — throw BatchListenerFailedException with the failing index so the error handler commits the successful prefix and retries or dead-letters from the failed record.

Q49. How do you propagate trace context through Kafka?

The W3C traceparent header is written into Kafka record headers by the instrumented producer and read by the instrumented consumer, creating a child span (or a span link for batches). With Spring Boot 3 and Micrometer Tracing, enable observation on KafkaTemplate and the listener container. Our outbox is a special case: the trace context must be stored with the outbox row and restored by the relay, otherwise the relay's own scheduled span becomes the parent.

Q50. Kafka vs RabbitMQ — how do you choose?

Kafka when you need high throughput, multiple independent consumers, replay, retention, event sourcing, stream processing or CDC. RabbitMQ when you need flexible routing (topic/headers exchanges), per-message acknowledgements, priorities, TTL, request/reply, and modest volumes with simpler operations. Many systems run both: Kafka for domain events, RabbitMQ or a DB queue for task distribution.

Q51. How does SQS differ from Kafka for a work queue?

SQS is fully managed with no partitions to size: a consumer receives a message, which becomes invisible for the visibility timeout; it deletes the message when done, or the message reappears for another consumer. Standard queues are at-least-once with best-effort order; FIFO queues order per message group and de-duplicate within five minutes. No replay, no consumer groups — fan-out is SNS → multiple SQS queues. Great for AWS-native task queues; poor for event streaming and replay.

Q52. What is a visibility timeout and what goes wrong if it is too short?

The period after ReceiveMessage during which the message is hidden from other consumers. If processing takes longer, the message reappears and a second consumer processes it in parallel — duplicates and races. Set it above the worst-case processing time, extend it with ChangeMessageVisibility for long jobs, and keep handlers idempotent. It is the same idea as a lease on a claimed row in a DB queue.

Q53. Explain RabbitMQ exchanges.

Producers publish to an exchange with a routing key; bindings route to queues. Direct: exact routing key match. Topic: wildcard patterns (orders.*.eu, # for many words). Fanout: every bound queue, routing key ignored. Headers: match on message headers. The default exchange routes by queue name. Dead-letter exchanges receive rejected, expired or overflowed messages.

Q54. How do you guarantee no message loss in RabbitMQ?

Durable exchange and queue (preferably a quorum queue), persistent messages (delivery mode 2), publisher confirms (and the mandatory flag or alternate exchange for unroutable messages), manual consumer acks sent only after processing, and a sensible prefetch. Plus idempotent consumers, because redelivery after a lost ack is still possible.

Q55. What is Kafka Streams and how is it different from a plain consumer?

A Java library for stateful stream processing: aggregations, windowing, joins, with local RocksDB state stores backed by compacted changelog topics, automatic partition-based scaling and exactly-once (exactly_once_v2). A plain consumer gives you records; you would have to build state, fault-tolerant recovery and joins yourself. It runs inside your application — no separate cluster like Flink or Spark.

Q56. KStream vs KTable?

A KStream is a record stream: every record is an independent event (two payments are two payments). A KTable is a changelog: each record is an update to the latest value for its key (a later address replaces the earlier one). stream.groupByKey().count() produces a KTable; table.toStream() turns updates back into a stream.

Q57. Why must topics be co-partitioned for a stream-table join?

The join happens locally inside each task: the task handling partition 3 of the stream must have partition 3 of the table, which only contains matching keys if both topics have the same partition count and the same partitioning by key. Otherwise Streams repartitions through an internal topic, or you use a GlobalKTable (full copy everywhere) for small reference data.

Q58. A consumer must call a slow external API per message. How do you design it?

Separate fetching from processing: keep the poll loop fast, process with bounded concurrency per key, pause() partitions when the internal queue is full and resume() when it drains, commit only completed contiguous offsets. Add timeouts, circuit breaker and retry with back-off; route permanently failing messages to a DLT. Or turn the work into a durable job queue (a DB table) that the consumer only enqueues into, which is often simpler.

Q59. What causes duplicate messages in Kafka-based systems?

Producer retries without idempotence, application-level resends after a timeout whose original actually succeeded, outbox relays crashing between send and marking sent, consumers crashing or being rebalanced after processing but before committing, and DLT replays. That is why idempotent consumers are non-negotiable with at-least-once delivery.

Q60. How do you replay events after fixing a consumer bug?

Stop the consumer group, reset offsets (kafka-consumer-groups.sh --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-10-30T00:00:00.000 --group audit-service --topic rp.audit.events --execute, or --to-offset, --shift-by), restart. The data must still be within retention, and consumers must be idempotent or the dedupe table must be cleared selectively. Alternatively use a new consumer group for a parallel rebuild.

Q61. How would you secure Kafka?

TLS for encryption in transit (and broker-to-broker), authentication with SASL (SCRAM, OAUTHBEARER) or mutual TLS, ACLs per principal on topics and groups (a service can write only its own topics), quotas to stop noisy clients, and encryption at rest at the disk level. Do not put secrets or unmasked personal data in events, because retention and replication multiply copies.

RefinePoint: services connect to the managed Kafka cluster over SSL, verifying the cluster's CA certificate (secrets/kafka-ca.pem), with credentials from the environment files. Topic prefixes (nonprod.) let environments share one cluster safely.

Q62. Tell me how you used Kafka in your project and one design decision you would defend.

"RefinePoint uses Kafka for three event streams — audit, run completed and notifications — produced through a transactional outbox and consumed by idempotent listeners with a consumed_events table. The decision I defend is restraint: Kafka only where one event has several consumers or must survive a consumer outage; everything else is a synchronous call. That kept the system debuggable for a solo developer, while the outbox means a Kafka outage is invisible to users — events wait in the table and catch up."

28. System Design Interview Round

The system design round decides the level you are hired at. A mid-level candidate draws boxes; a senior candidate drives the conversation, asks the questions that change the design, puts numbers on the board, and spends most of the time on the two or three places where the system will actually break. This chapter gives you a repeatable framework, the numbers you must know by heart, and fifteen complete designs — each with scale assumptions, components, data flow, failure handling and the follow-up questions interviewers ask next. Several of them are systems we built in RefinePoint, which gives you real answers to "have you built something like this?".

28.1 The framework

Step Minutes (of 45) What you say and produce
Requirements 5 3–5 core features in scope, explicitly out of scope items; non-functional: scale, latency, availability, consistency, durability, security, multi-region
Estimates 3–5 Read and write QPS (average and peak), storage per year, bandwidth, cache size — only what drives a decision
API 3–5 REST/gRPC signatures with idempotency keys, pagination, auth; async events if any
Data model 5 Main tables/documents, primary keys, partition keys, indexes; SQL vs NoSQL with a reason
High-level design 7–10 Clients → edge (CDN, LB, gateway) → services → stores, queues, caches; walk one request end to end
Deep dives 10–15 The parts the interviewer cares about: hot keys, ordering, consistency, fan-out, exactly-once
Bottlenecks and failures 5 What happens when each box dies; retries, timeouts, back-pressure, degradation
Trade-offs 2–3 What you chose, what you gave up, how it evolves at 10x

What interviewers score: scoping (did you ask before drawing), quantitative reasoning, sound defaults (stateless services, idempotency, caches with invalidation), depth in at least one area, failure thinking, and communication (you drive, you check in, you name trade-offs out loud).

Interview tip: say "let me make an assumption and you tell me if it's wrong" instead of waiting. State numbers as round powers of ten. When you pick a technology, add the reason in one clause: "PostgreSQL, because orders need transactions and the write rate fits one primary".

28.2 Back-of-envelope numbers

Quantity Value Use it for
Seconds per day 86,400 ≈ 10⁵ 1M requests/day ≈ 12 QPS; 100M/day ≈ 1,200 QPS
Peak factor 2–5× average Size for peak, not average
L1 cache / main memory reference 1 ns / 100 ns Why in-memory caches matter
SSD random read ~100 µs ~10k random reads/s per thread
Read 1 MB sequentially from memory / SSD ~10 µs / ~200 µs Scans vs lookups
Round trip in a datacenter ~0.5 ms Each service hop costs this plus processing
Round trip cross-continent ~150 ms Why multi-region reads need local replicas
Redis GET < 1 ms, 100k+ ops/s per node Cache and counters
PostgreSQL single primary thousands to ~20k simple writes/s; reads scale with replicas When to shard
Kafka cluster hundreds of thousands to millions msgs/s Event fan-out
One Spring Boot instance 1k–5k simple RPS; far less with heavy DB work Instance count
Typical row / event / tweet 100 B – 1 KB Storage
Image / document 100 KB – few MB Object storage, CDN 
Storage example: 10M new rows/day x 500 bytes = 5 GB/day ~ 1.8 TB/year (+ indexes ~2x, + replicas x3)
Bandwidth example: 1,000 QPS x 50 KB response = 50 MB/s ~ 400 Mbit/s egress
Cache example: 20% of 100M objects x 1 KB = 20 GB -> fits in a small Redis cluster

28.3 Building blocks you will reuse

Need Default choice Why / caveat
Stateless scale Load balancer + N instances State goes to DB/cache; sticky sessions only for WebSockets
Read scale Cache-aside (Redis) + read replicas Invalidation and replica lag
Write scale Partition/shard by a key (tenant, user) Cross-shard queries and re-sharding pain
Even key distribution Consistent hashing with virtual nodes Adding a node moves ~1/N keys
Decoupling, fan-out Kafka/SQS Eventual consistency, idempotent consumers
Atomic DB + event Transactional outbox At-least-once delivery
Distributed workflow Saga (orchestrated or choreographed) Compensations instead of 2PC
Unique IDs UUIDv7 / Snowflake (time + node + sequence) Sortable, no DB round trip
Large files Object storage + presigned URLs Never through the app servers
Search Elasticsearch/OpenSearch, Postgres full-text for small scale Index lag
Protection Rate limiting, circuit breakers, timeouts, bulkheads Fail fast instead of cascading

28.4 Design a URL shortener

Q1. Design a URL shortener like bit.ly.

Requirements. Create a short link for a long URL (optional custom alias, expiry); redirect short → long; basic click analytics. Non-functional: redirects extremely fast (p99 < 20 ms at the edge) and highly available; reads ≫ writes (100:1); links must never collide.

Estimates. 100M new links/month ≈ 40 writes/s (peak 200). 10B redirects/month ≈ 4,000 reads/s (peak 20k). Storage: 100M × 12 months × 5 years × 500 B ≈ 3 TB. Code length: base62 with 7 characters = 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion codes, plenty.

API.

POST /api/links   {longUrl, alias?, expiresAt?}  -> 201 {code, shortUrl}   (Idempotency-Key header)
GET  /{code}                                     -> 301/302 Location: longUrl
GET  /api/links/{code}/stats                     -> clicks by day, referrer, country

Data model. links(code PK, long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at); key-value access by code, so either PostgreSQL (fine at this write rate) or DynamoDB/Cassandra partitioned by code. Clicks go to an append-only analytics store, not the links table.

Code generation options.

Approach How Pros Cons
Hash (MD5/SHA of URL), take 7 chars Deterministic Same URL → same code Collisions need check-and-retry
Counter + base62 Global sequence encoded No collisions, short Predictable codes; sequence is a hot spot
Range allocation Each app instance leases a block of 10,000 ids from a DB/ZooKeeper counter No per-request coordination Gaps on restart (harmless)
Random 7 chars + unique insert INSERT ... ON CONFLICT retry Unpredictable Retry at high fill ratio

I would use range allocation + base62, optionally shuffled through a bijective permutation so codes are not guessable.

Flow. Redirect: edge cache → Redis (hit rate > 90% because traffic follows a power law) → DB on miss, populate cache. The click is emitted asynchronously to Kafka so analytics never slows a redirect.

Failure handling. Redis down → read from DB replicas (degraded latency). Analytics pipeline down → clicks buffer in Kafka. Allocator down → instances still have leased ranges.

Q2. 301 or 302 redirect?

301 (permanent) lets browsers and CDNs cache the redirect — less load, but you lose click counts after the first visit and cannot change the target. 302/307 (temporary) sends every click through you — accurate analytics and editable targets. Most commercial shorteners use 302 for analytics; use 301 when cost matters more than counts.

Q3. How do you handle a viral link getting 100k requests per second?

It is a hot key. Serve it from the CDN with a short TTL (even 5–10 s absorbs nearly everything), keep an in-process cache in front of Redis for the top keys, and make analytics counting asynchronous and aggregated (count in memory per instance, flush every second).

Q4. How do you prevent abuse (phishing, spam)?

Rate-limit link creation per account and IP, check long URLs against safe-browsing lists at creation and periodically, allow disabling a code (cache invalidation via short TTL or explicit delete), and require authentication for custom aliases.

28.5 Design a rate limiter

Q5. Design a distributed rate limiter for an API platform.

Requirements. Limit requests per client identity (API key, user, IP) per time window; return 429 with Retry-After; different limits per plan; low overhead (< 1 ms added); works across many gateway instances; fail-open or fail-closed configurable.

Algorithms.

Algorithm State per key Behaviour Weakness
Fixed window counter count, window start Simple INCR with TTL Burst of 2× at window boundary
Sliding window log timestamps of each request Exact Memory O(requests)
Sliding window counter current + previous window counts Weighted estimate, smooth Approximation (good enough)
Token bucket tokens, last refill time Allows bursts up to capacity, steady refill rate Two parameters to tune
Leaky bucket queue Smooths output to a constant rate Adds latency (queueing)

Token bucket in one line: tokens refill at rate r up to capacity b; a request takes one token or is rejected. Refill is computed lazily on access: tokens = min(b, tokens + (now − last) × r).

Distributed version. Keep bucket state in Redis keyed by rl:{apiKey}; run the refill-and-take logic as a Lua script so it is atomic (no read-modify-write race between gateways). Set a TTL so idle keys vanish. Redis Cluster shards by key, so load spreads. For latency, a hybrid: each gateway keeps a local bucket with a share of the limit and syncs with Redis periodically (less accurate, much cheaper).

Failure handling. Redis unavailable → fail open (allow, log, alert) for most APIs, fail closed for expensive or security-sensitive endpoints (login, OTP). Timeouts on the Redis call must be tiny (a few ms).

RefinePoint: our api-gateway's RateLimitFilter is a token bucket per caller held in a ConcurrentHashMap: 300 requests/minute per API key, 900 per signed-in user (the web app asks for a page's parts at once), and 1,800 per IP address as a backstop. Each bucket holds a minute's requests and refills evenly. Over the limit the answer is 429 with Retry-After, and every response carries X-RateLimit-Limit and X-RateLimit-Remaining. Health checks, CORS preflights and Paddle webhooks are not counted. Because the buckets live in each gateway's memory, with several gateways each one limits what passes through it — the honest trade-off: zero network cost and no Redis dependency, at the price of a global limit that is N × the configured one. When we run more than one gateway, moving the buckets to Redis with a Lua script is the planned change.

Q6. Where should rate limiting live: gateway, service or both?

At the gateway for coarse protection per identity (cheap, before any work is done) and in the service for business quotas that need domain knowledge (reconciliations per month, AI calls per workspace). The gateway protects capacity; the service enforces the product plan.

Q7. How do you rate-limit across regions?

Exact global limits need cross-region coordination, which adds latency. Usually you split the limit per region (each region gets a share and enforces locally) or sync counters asynchronously and accept small over-admission.

Q8. What headers and behaviour should a well-behaved rate limiter expose?

429 status, Retry-After (seconds), and limit/remaining/reset headers (X-RateLimit-* or the IETF RateLimit fields). Clients should back off with jitter. Distinguish 429 (your quota) from 503 (server overloaded) so clients react correctly.

28.6 Design a notification system

Q9. Design a notification system that sends email, SMS and push notifications.

Requirements. Many producer services send notifications; channels email, SMS, push, in-app; user preferences and opt-outs; templates and localisation; retries; no duplicates where possible; priority (OTP now, digest later); delivery tracking.

Estimates. 10M notifications/day ≈ 120/s average, peaks 10× for campaigns; OTPs need seconds of latency, marketing can take hours.

Flow. Producers emit an event with recipient, type and data (not rendered text). The notification service checks preferences, rate-limits per user (no 50 pushes in a minute), renders the template, and enqueues per-channel jobs. Channel workers call providers with timeouts and record each attempt.

Failure handling. Provider error → retry with exponential back-off and jitter; after N attempts, dead-letter and try a fallback provider or channel. Separate queues per channel and priority give bulkheads: an SMS outage or a marketing burst cannot delay OTP emails. Deduplicate with a notification id (idempotency key) passed to providers that support it and checked in the delivery log. Provider callbacks (bounce, delivered) update status; hard bounces disable the address.

RefinePoint: any service publishes a notification for a person to the rp.notifications Kafka topic through the outbox. alert-notify-service consumes it twice: its normal consumer group stores each notification once in the person's inbox, and a per-instance group (auto.offset.reset=latest) pushes it to that person's open pages over the live stream that instance holds, so any number of instances can serve live connections. Alerts can also go out by email (EmailSender), outgoing webhooks (WebhookSender) and chat channels. Email addresses in logs are masked with LogMasks.email().

Q10. How do you guarantee a notification is sent exactly once?

You cannot across an external provider; aim for at-least-once with deduplication. Assign a notification id at creation, record "sent" in the delivery log keyed by it, and check before sending. The gap — crash after the provider accepted but before recording — is narrowed by provider idempotency keys where supported. For OTPs a rare duplicate is acceptable; for a charge it is not.

Q11. How do you send a campaign to 50 million users without hurting transactional traffic?

Separate priority queues and worker pools, throttle the campaign to provider rate limits, fan out in chunks (a job enumerates audience pages and enqueues batches), and schedule by recipient time zone. Transactional queues keep reserved capacity.

Q12. How do you deliver in-app notifications in real time to many server instances?

Clients hold a WebSocket or server-sent events connection to some instance. Either every instance subscribes to all notification events and pushes to the connections it holds (broadcast, simple — our approach), or a connection registry (Redis: user → instance) routes each message to the right instance. Missed messages are read from the stored inbox on reconnect.

28.7 Design a distributed job scheduler

Q13. Design a distributed job scheduler (cron at scale) that runs each job exactly once per schedule.

Requirements. Users define jobs (cron or interval, time zone, payload); jobs run on time across a cluster of workers; a job never runs twice concurrently; missed runs handled by policy; retries with back-off; time limits; cancel; history and logs.

Data model.

jobs(id, org_id, cron, time_zone, next_due_at, misfire_policy, max_retries, timeout_s,
     running_execution_id NULL, enabled)
job_executions(id, job_id, status, attempt, instance, heartbeat_at, started_at, finished_at, error)
CREATE INDEX ON jobs (next_due_at) WHERE enabled AND running_execution_id IS NULL;

Claiming. Every few seconds each instance runs, in one short transaction:

SELECT id FROM jobs
 WHERE enabled AND running_execution_id IS NULL AND next_due_at <= now()
 ORDER BY next_due_at
 LIMIT 10
 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
-- then: insert execution, set running_execution_id and next_due_at = next fire time after now, commit

SKIP LOCKED makes concurrent instances skip rows another instance is claiming, so there is no leader and no double claim; throughput scales by adding instances.

Failure handling. A worker crash leaves an execution "running"; a watchdog fails executions whose instance stopped heart-beating (stale after a few minutes) and clears the claim so the next run can happen. Timeouts cancel the task (TIMED_OUT). Failed attempts are retried with doubling back-off up to max_retries. Misfires (service down at due time) are either made up by one run or skipped by policy, and the next due time is always the first one after now — never a storm of catch-up runs.

RefinePoint: this is our job-service JobScheduler almost line for line: claims with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, running_execution_id so a job runs at most once at a time, a watchdog for time limits, cancellations and stale instances, doubling back-off retries, and misfire policy (make up once or SKIP). It also refuses to run anything in a locked workspace (licence suspended) and simply tries again at the next due time. run-service, the export worker and the datasource refresh worker use the same claim pattern.

Q14. Why not Quartz or a single leader?

Quartz clustered mode also uses DB row locks and works, but brings its own schema and API. A single leader (elected via ZooKeeper/etcd or a DB lock) is simple but caps throughput at one node and needs failover. SKIP LOCKED claiming gives active-active workers with nothing but the database you already run. At very high scale (millions of jobs per minute) you shard the job table by time bucket or use a dedicated system (Temporal, Kafka-based delay queues).

Q15. How do you handle time zones and DST in cron jobs?

Store the cron expression and an IANA zone, compute the next fire time in that zone with ZonedDateTime, and persist it as UTC. On DST spring-forward a 02:30 job does not exist that day — decide (run at 03:00 or skip); on fall-back avoid running twice by computing "next after now" from the stored last fire time.

Q16. How do you make job execution exactly-once?

Claiming makes start-at-most-once per schedule, but a crash mid-job forces a choice between rerun (at-least-once) and give up. So make job bodies idempotent (upserts, per-run keys) and accept at-least-once with retries. Exactly-once effects come from idempotency, not from the scheduler.

28.8 Design a file ingestion and processing pipeline

Q17. Design a pipeline that accepts large CSV/Excel files (up to several GB) and processes them reliably.

Requirements. Upload by browser, API, SFTP or email; validate; transform; load; report progress and row-level errors; re-upload must not double-load; a big file from one customer must not starve others.

Estimates. 50k files/day, median 5 MB, p99 2 GB: about 500 GB/day of raw data. A server cannot hold a 2 GB file in the heap, so everything must stream.

Key decisions.

  1. Bytes bypass the app. Clients upload straight to object storage with presigned, multipart URLs (resumable, each part retried). The API only records metadata and a checksum.
  2. Durable claim. A row in files with status QUEUED → PROCESSING → DONE/FAILED; workers claim with SKIP LOCKED or consume a Kafka message carrying a reference (claim check).
  3. Streaming, not loading. Stream CSV line by line; for .xlsx use a SAX/event parser (Apache POI XSSFReader), because the DOM model of a 500 MB workbook needs many gigabytes of heap. Or hand the file to a columnar engine (DuckDB read_csv) that spills to disk.
  4. Idempotency. Key on (tenant, source, SHA-256 of the file). The same file twice answers "already loaded"; load into a staging table, then swap or insert in one transaction, so a crash leaves nothing half-visible.
  5. Row errors. Do not fail the file for one bad row unless the customer asks for it; write rejects with line number and reason to an error file; abort only above a threshold.
  6. Fairness. Per-tenant concurrency caps and dedicated queues so one tenant's 2 GB file cannot occupy every worker.

Failure handling. Worker dies → heartbeat expires, the file is reclaimed and restarted from staging (clean up first). Corrupt file → FAILED with a human-readable reason; no retry. Out of memory → process exit and restart with a lower concurrency, not a half-alive JVM (-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError). Virus scan and size and type checks happen before parsing.

RefinePoint: ingest-service routes files arriving through uploads, the API, a hosted SFTP inbox, watched folders and inbound email to a process side. Processing happens in the run service: DuckDB runs in-process per run, prepares, types, converts currency and filters in SQL, and spills to disk beyond RYFN_DUCKDB_MEMORY_LIMIT (default 40% of the machine, shared among the runs going on). Rules compile to DuckDB SQL through SqlCompiler; functions without a native form run their Java code inside DuckDB. If ingest is down, files sent by SFTP or API wait and routes resume when it is back.

Q18. Why is DuckDB attractive compared to loading rows into PostgreSQL or the JVM heap?

DuckDB is an in-process columnar, vectorised SQL engine: joins and aggregates over millions of rows run in seconds, it spills to disk, needs no server, and each run gets an isolated working set that vanishes afterwards. Loading the same rows into the OLTP database bloats tables and WAL and competes with user queries; holding them in Java objects costs 10–50× the raw size in heap and GC pressure.

Q19. How do you report progress on a long-running file job?

Write coarse progress (rows processed, phase) to the job row every few seconds, not per row. Clients poll a status endpoint or receive server-sent events. Return 202 Accepted with a status URL from the start endpoint; never hold an HTTP request open for a long job.

Q20. How do you handle a file with a changed schema (a new column, renamed header)?

Map by header name rather than position, profile a sample (types, null rates) before the full load, ignore unknown columns with a warning, and fail fast with a clear message when a required mapped column is missing. Keep mapping definitions versioned per source.

28.9 Design a payment and subscription system with webhooks

Q21. Design subscription billing using a payment provider such as Stripe or Paddle.

Requirements. Plans and prices; checkout; recurring charges, upgrades, cancellation; entitlements (what a workspace may do) follow the subscription; invoices; no card data on our servers (PCI scope stays with the provider).

Data model.

plans(id, name, limits, provider_price_id)
payment_orders(id, org_id, plan_id, created_by, status)        -- our record of an intent to buy
org_subscriptions(org_id, plan_id, provider_subscription_id, status, current_period_end)
webhook_events(event_id PK, type, processed_at)                -- dedupe

Rules that matter.

  • The webhook is the source of truth, not the browser redirect. A success page proves nothing; the user may close the tab before it loads, or fake it.
  • Verify before parsing: HMAC signature over the raw body, plus a timestamp tolerance to stop replays.
  • Idempotent and order-tolerant. Providers retry and may deliver out of order. Dedupe on event id in the same transaction as the change; compare occurred_at or fetch current state from the provider API when in doubt.
  • Return 2xx only after committing. On failure answer 5xx and let the provider retry.
  • Reconcile. A nightly job compares provider subscriptions with local rows, because a webhook outage must not become permanent drift.
  • Dunning. A failed renewal moves to past_due with a grace period before the workspace is limited.

RefinePoint: billing-service's PaddleWebhookProcessor runs while Paddle waits for the answer: anything that fails answers 500 and Paddle sends the event again. Three defences come first: the source address must be in Paddle's published IP list (PaddleWebhookSources, refreshed hourly), the Paddle-Signature (ts=...;h1=...) must verify, with one h1 per secret during rotation, and it must be within five minutes. Nothing the buyer's browser could set is trusted: the plan comes from the price paid and the workspace from the PaymentOrder we created, never from the transaction's custom data. Each event is processed once by its id, recorded in the same transaction as the change. A workspace already paying is never moved onto a second subscription: its other checkouts are cancelled, and a duplicate that is paid anyway is cancelled and refunded (DuplicatePurchases). Plan limits are enforced by PlanLimits / PlanLimitExceededException, and if billing is down plan checks are allowed and logged, because a billing outage must not stop people working.

Q22. What if the webhook arrives before your own API call finishes?

It happens: the provider can call back before you have stored its id. Create your own order row before redirecting to the provider and pass the order id as a reference, so the webhook always has something to attach to. If it finds nothing, answer 5xx so it is retried rather than dropping it.

Q23. Should a billing outage block the product?

Usually not. Treat plan checks as fail-open with a logged warning and a short-lived cached entitlement, so paying customers keep working. Fail closed only for actions that spend real money for you, such as high-cost AI calls beyond a cached limit.

Q24. How do you handle upgrades, downgrades and proration?

Let the provider compute proration; upgrades take effect immediately, downgrades at the period end, because limits may no longer fit (more seats than the new plan allows). Store the pending plan, and on the period-change webhook apply it and warn or restrict rather than deleting anything.

28.10 Design a multi-tenant SaaS

Q25. Design the tenancy model of a B2B SaaS application.

Requirements. Thousands of workspaces, strict isolation, per-tenant plan limits and roles, no noisy neighbours, data deletion on request, simple operations for a small team.

Model Isolation Cost Ops Best for
Shared tables with org_id Logical (code, RLS) Lowest Simple migrations Many small tenants
Schema per tenant Better Medium Migrations × N schemas, catalogue bloat Hundreds of tenants
Database per tenant Strong High Fleet management Regulated or very large tenants
Hybrid Tiered Varies Most complex Large tenants on dedicated hardware

Isolation in depth. Bake the tenant into the type system (BaseOrgEntity), resolve it once per request from a verified identity, and pass it down. Add a safety net: PostgreSQL row-level security or Hibernate filters. Composite indexes start with org_id, and caches and object-storage paths include it. Background jobs and event consumers must carry the tenant explicitly, because there is no HTTP request to read it from.

Noisy neighbours. Per-caller rate limits, per-tenant concurrency caps, dedicated worker queues for big customers, and statement timeouts. Partition huge tables by hash of org_id.

Tenant lifecycle. Provisioning is one row plus defaults, not infrastructure. Deletion is a durable, repeated request to every service until each has confirmed.

RefinePoint: paths are org-scoped, X-Org-Code names the workspace, OrgAccessInterceptor and OrgContextService enforce and carry it, and every tenant table has org_id through BaseOrgEntity. Keycloak says who the caller is; workspace roles live in identity-service and are cached for 30 seconds. A workspace's concurrent runs are capped (RUNS_PER_WORKSPACE, default 4), a workspace can be pinned to a dedicated run queue (RUN_QUEUES=acme) for a machine of its own, and deleting a workspace makes identity ask every service to purge (workspace_purges), again until each has.

Q26. How do you prove one tenant cannot read another tenant's data?

Automated cross-tenant tests: create two orgs, then call every endpoint as org A with org B's ids and expect 403/404. Enforce by construction (repository methods require orgId), and add RLS as a second layer so one forgotten WHERE is not a breach. Return 404 rather than 403 where existence itself is sensitive.

Q27. How would you add RLS to a shared-schema PostgreSQL design?

ALTER TABLE breaks ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY;
CREATE POLICY tenant_only ON breaks USING (org_id = current_setting('app.org_id')::uuid);

Set the variable per transaction with SET LOCAL app.org_id = ... (never SET, because a pooled connection would keep it), and use a non-owner role, since table owners bypass RLS unless FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY is set.

Q28. A huge tenant dominates your database. What now?

Measure first (pg_stat_statements by tenant). Then hash-partition by org_id, move that tenant's heavy reads to a replica, give its workers a dedicated queue, and as a last step move it to its own database — easy only if a routing layer maps tenant to datasource (AbstractRoutingDataSource).

28.11 Design an e-commerce order system with a saga

Q29. Design order placement across order, inventory, payment and shipping services.

Requirements. Place an order atomically in business terms: reserve stock, charge, ship. No overselling, no charge without an order. 2,000 orders/s at peak, browsing 100× that.

Each service owns its database, so a single ACID transaction is unavailable and 2PC would couple availability of all four. Use a saga: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action.

Orchestration Choreography
Control Central state machine Services react to each other's events
Visibility One place to see the state Spread out; needs tracing
Coupling Orchestrator knows every step Low, but cycles are easy to create
Use when 4+ steps, business-critical 2–3 steps

Key details. Commands and events go through an outbox; every step is idempotent (keyed by order id plus step) because retries are guaranteed. Saga state is persisted, so the orchestrator can crash and resume. Compensations must be retried until they succeed, and a stuck saga alerts a human. Order the steps so the hardest to undo comes last: reserve stock (easy to release) before charging (refund is visible to the customer) before shipping (cannot be undone).

Inventory. UPDATE stock SET available = available - ? WHERE sku = ? AND available >= ? — the conditional update prevents overselling without a read-modify-write race. Reservations carry an expiry, and a sweeper releases abandoned ones. Hot SKUs in a flash sale: pre-load counts in Redis with an atomic Lua decrement as a gate, then settle in the database asynchronously.

Q30. Saga vs 2PC — why not distributed transactions?

2PC holds locks across services until the coordinator decides, so one slow participant blocks all, and a crashed coordinator can leave locks in doubt. Many modern stores and brokers do not take part in XA at all. Sagas give up isolation (intermediate states are visible) and gain availability. You compensate for the isolation loss with semantic locks such as a PENDING status.

Q31. What isolation problems do sagas have?

Lost updates and dirty reads between steps: another saga can read a reservation that will be released. Countermeasures: semantic locks (status flags), commutative updates, versioned rows, and re-reading state before the pivot step — the step after which the saga can only move forward.

Q32. What if a compensation fails?

Retry with back-off (it must be idempotent). After N attempts, park the saga in a COMPENSATION_FAILED state, alert, and give operations a tool to resolve it. Never drop it silently: money and stock have to balance, and a scheduled reconciliation job should be able to detect the mismatch independently.

28.12 Design a chat system

Q33. Design a WhatsApp/Slack-style chat system.

Requirements. 1:1 and group chat, online presence, read receipts, offline delivery, history, media by link. 100M daily users, 50 messages/user/day ≈ 60k messages/s, peak 200k; p99 delivery under 500 ms when both are online.

Data model. messages(conversation_id, message_id, sender_id, body, sent_at), partition key conversation_id, clustering key a time-sortable message_id (Snowflake, or a per-conversation sequence). Wide-column stores fit this append-heavy, time-range pattern. Each user also keeps last_read_message_id per conversation.

Flow. The client sends with a client-generated id; the service persists it, acks the sender (one tick), then publishes to Kafka keyed by conversation, which preserves per-conversation order. Fan-out looks up each member's gateway in Redis and delivers (two ticks); offline members get a push and sync on reconnect by asking "messages after my last id".

Failure handling. A gateway dies → clients reconnect elsewhere with back-off and jitter, then resync from last_seen_id, so at-least-once delivery plus client-side dedupe on message id gives a clean view. Thundering herd on reconnect is limited with jitter and connection-rate limits at the load balancer.

Q34. How do you handle a group with 100,000 members?

Do not fan out to all on write. For very large channels, deliver only to members currently connected (per-gateway subscription to the channel) and let others read on open, like a fan-out-on-read feed. Limit typing indicators and receipts, which are the real traffic multipliers: aggregate counts rather than per-user ticks.

Q35. WebSocket vs SSE vs long polling?

WebSocket: full-duplex, the right fit for chat. SSE: server-to-client over HTTP, auto-reconnects, simple, works through most proxies; ideal for notifications (we use SseEmitter for the inbox). Long polling: a fallback that wastes connections and latency. WebSockets need sticky connections and a load balancer with long idle timeouts.

Q36. How does presence work without crushing the system?

Clients heartbeat every 30 s; a Redis key with a TTL (presence:{user}) expires if they stop. Publish changes only to users who currently view that person, debounced, and fetch presence lazily for the visible contacts rather than broadcasting to all friends.

28.13 Design a news feed

Q37. Design a social media news feed.

Requirements. Post, follow, read a personalised reverse-chronological or ranked feed. 500M daily users, 10 feed reads/day ≈ 60k reads/s, 2 posts/user/week ≈ 2k posts/s; p99 feed read under 200 ms.

Fan-out on write (push) Fan-out on read (pull)
On post Insert post id into each follower's feed cache Nothing extra
On read Read prebuilt list — fast Merge recent posts of all followees — slow
Bad case Celebrity with 50M followers User following thousands

Answer: hybrid. Push for ordinary authors; for celebrities (above a follower threshold) skip fan-out and merge their recent posts at read time.

Details. Feed caches store only ids (a few hundred per user), hydrated on read through a post cache; inactive users are skipped at fan-out and rebuilt on next login. Pagination uses a cursor (last post id), never OFFSET, because new posts shift the pages. Ranking: candidate generation (a few hundred) then a light model scoring recency and affinity.

Q38. How do you handle deleting a post or unfollowing?

Filter at read time: hydration drops deleted posts, and a lazy cleanup removes stale ids. Fanning out deletes to millions of feeds is wasteful when a read filter is correct immediately.

Q39. How do you survive a fan-out backlog during a viral event?

Kafka absorbs the burst; feeds become a little stale, not broken. Prioritise active followers, autoscale consumers on lag, and let the read path merge the author's recent posts if fan-out is behind.

28.14 Design search autocomplete

Q40. Design type-ahead suggestions for a search box.

Requirements. Top 5–10 suggestions per prefix, under 50 ms including network, popularity-ranked, updated within hours; 10B searches/day, and a client request per keystroke (debounced) gives ~200k QPS at peak.

Trie with precomputed top-k at each node (lookup is O(length of prefix))
 (root)
  └─ s  [spring, sql, saga]
     └─ p [spring, spark, spa]
        └─ r [spring, sprint, spread]

Design. Precompute: each trie node stores its top-k, so reads never traverse the subtree. Build offline every few hours from aggregated counts with time decay; ship immutable snapshots to read-only in-memory nodes, sharded by prefix (by weighted ranges rather than alphabet, because "s" is much heavier than "x"). Cache short prefixes at the CDN and browser for minutes: they make up most traffic and rarely change. Filter blocked terms at build time, and blend in personal history on the client side.

Failure handling. Nodes are stateless replicas of a snapshot, so losing one is a non-event; a bad build is rolled back by pointing at the previous snapshot. On timeout the UI simply shows no suggestions: autocomplete is never allowed to break search.

Q41. How do you surface breaking trends within minutes?

Add a small real-time layer: a stream job counts queries over sliding windows and keeps a hot-prefix map that is merged with the static trie at read time, and is discarded when the next snapshot includes them.

Q42. Elasticsearch completion suggester or a custom trie?

Start with the suggester (or a Postgres pg_trgm/prefix index at small scale): quick and handles fuzziness. A custom in-memory trie wins at very high QPS with strict latency and full control of ranking, at the cost of a build pipeline.

28.15 Design a distributed cache

Q43. Design a distributed in-memory cache like Redis Cluster or Memcached.

Requirements. GET/SET/DELETE with TTL, sub-millisecond latency, terabytes across many nodes, node failures tolerated, horizontal scale; eventual consistency is acceptable.

Partitioning. Consistent hashing with virtual nodes spreads load and moves only ~1/N keys when a node joins. (Redis Cluster uses a variant: 16,384 hash slots mapped to nodes, with MOVED redirects.) Eviction: LRU or LFU per node with a memory limit; the classic implementation is a hash map plus doubly linked list, O(1) get and put. Expiry: lazy on access plus periodic sampling. Replication: asynchronous to a replica, so a failover may lose the last writes — acceptable for a cache. Failure detection: gossip heartbeats; on primary loss, the replica is promoted.

Client-side issues interviewers probe.

Problem What happens Fix
Stampede Popular key expires, thousands hit the DB Single-flight lock per key, early probabilistic refresh, serve stale
Penetration Queries for keys that do not exist bypass the cache Cache negative results briefly, Bloom filter
Avalanche Many keys expire at once, or a node is lost TTL jitter, multi-level cache, circuit breaker on the DB
Hot key One key saturates a node Local in-process cache, replicate to reads, split the key
Big key A 50 MB value blocks a single-threaded node Split it, compress it, stop caching it

RefinePoint: at our scale a local TtlCache is enough, for example workspace role answers cached 30 seconds so a role change takes effect quickly and identity outages are survivable for a moment. A distributed cache is not free: it is one more system to run and another failure mode, so we would add Redis only when several instances truly need to share a hot read.

Q44. Cache-aside, write-through, write-behind?

Cache-aside: the app reads the cache, loads on miss, and invalidates on write — simple and the default. Write-through: writes go through the cache to the DB synchronously — always fresh, slower writes. Write-behind: the cache acks then flushes asynchronously — fast writes, data at risk on a crash. Update the DB then delete the cache entry; deleting first opens a window where a concurrent read repopulates stale data.

Q45. Why is Redis single-threaded for commands and still fast?

Commands run on one thread in memory with no locks, so there is no contention; I/O multiplexing (and threaded network I/O since 6.0) handles many connections. The cost is that one slow command (KEYS *, a big SMEMBERS) blocks everyone, so use SCAN and avoid big keys. Details in chapter 25.

28.16 Design an idempotent payment API

Q46. Design a payment API that never charges a customer twice, even with client retries.

Requirements. POST /payments may be retried by clients after timeouts; each business payment charges at most once; concurrent duplicates handled; the response to a retry equals the original; downstream PSP calls can time out with an unknown result.

Data model.

CREATE TABLE idempotency_keys (
  org_id uuid, key text, request_hash text, status text,   -- IN_PROGRESS, COMPLETED
  response_code int, response_body jsonb, created_at timestamptz,
  PRIMARY KEY (org_id, key));
payments(id, org_id, amount, currency, status, psp_reference, ...)  -- CREATED -> SUBMITTED -> SUCCEEDED/FAILED/UNKNOWN

The rules.

  1. The insert is the lock. The unique primary key decides who processes; losers read the stored result. Scope the key by tenant.
  2. Compare request hashes. The same key with a different body is a client bug: 422.
  3. Never hold a DB transaction open across the PSP call. Commit intent first, call, then record. A connection held during an external call is an outage waiting to happen.
  4. Pass your payment id to the PSP as its idempotency key, so our own retries cannot double-charge.
  5. Unknown is a real state. A PSP timeout does not mean failure. Mark UNKNOWN, and have a recovery job query the PSP by reference. Never blindly retry with a new key.
  6. Money as BigDecimal or integer minor units, never double; an append-only ledger with double-entry rows for audit.
  7. Expire keys after 24–72 hours (retry window), in a scheduled sweep.

Q47. How do you recover a request that crashed between PSP success and local commit?

The key is stuck IN_PROGRESS and the payment is SUBMITTED with no result. A recovery worker finds rows older than a threshold, asks the PSP by our reference, and completes or fails the payment accordingly. The webhook from the PSP can do the same job, which is why both paths must be idempotent. Daily reconciliation against the PSP settlement file is the final safety net.

Q48. Should the client or the server generate the idempotency key?

The client, because only it knows that two requests are the same intent: a UUID generated once per user action and reused on retries. If the server derived it from content, two legitimate identical payments (two coffees) would be merged. For internal event-driven calls, derive it from the event id.

Q49. What happens with two concurrent requests with the same key?

Both attempt the insert. PostgreSQL serialises on the unique index: the second blocks until the first commits, then ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING returns zero rows. It reads the row, sees IN_PROGRESS and answers 409 or waits briefly; once COMPLETED it replays the response. No application-level lock or Redis is required for correctness.

28.17 Design a reconciliation platform end to end

Q50. Your own system as a design question: design a multi-tenant financial reconciliation SaaS.

Requirements. Tenants define processes: two sides (bank statement vs ledger), field mappings, match rules, tolerances. Data arrives by upload, SFTP, email or API. Runs match records and produce matched pairs and breaks (exceptions), which users review, approve and close at month end. Non-functional: exact results (financial), full audit trail, tenant isolation, millions of rows per run, runs scale independently of the API, solo-operable.

Estimates. 1,000 workspaces × 5 processes × 1 run/day = 5,000 runs/day, peaks at month end (5× or more). Typical run 100k rows a side, big runs 5–10M. Result rows ≈ 1B/month without retention, so results need per-workspace retention and partitioning.

Engine design. Two-sided data does not fit a naive nested loop: 1M × 1M is impossible.
