Provider client WireMock or MockRestServiceServer: request shape, 429, timeout, streaming Yes
Output parsing Feed malformed JSON, code fences, truncated output, wrong types Yes
Business flow Stub LlmClient with canned responses; test retry and fallback Yes
Model quality Golden dataset: inputs with expected outputs or scoring rules; report precision, recall and pass rate No: statistical
Safety Prompt-injection and data-leak cases as adversarial dataset Mostly
Production Sample and review, acceptance rate, drift, cost per call Monitor

Rules: never assert exact model text; assert structure and properties (valid JSON, chosen column exists, amount unchanged), or score with an evaluator. Pin the model version and record it with results. Run evaluation on any prompt or model change, and gate on a threshold rather than 100%; compare to the previous baseline. Live eval calls cost money and are slow, so run them nightly or on prompt changes rather than on every commit. Record and replay responses so that tests of everything else stay free and deterministic.

RefinePoint: LlmClient being an interface means that AI features are tested with ScriptedLlm, a stand-in model that answers with the next prepared reply and remembers every LlmRequest it was asked, so tests assert both what was sent and how the reply was handled, and never call a model. The draft tests feed messy output on purpose, such as "Sure! Here you go:" followed by a fenced JSON block containing a } inside a string, to prove JsonExtractor copes. Provider mapping is tested separately through LlmClientsTest.

30.15 A senior's testing strategy for a microservice

Level Scope Count and speed Runs
Unit Domain logic, calculators, parsers, state transitions Many, ms Every commit
Slice Controllers (validation, status, security), JSON Dozens, seconds Every commit
Integration Service + real PostgreSQL + real migrations, repositories, transactions, concurrency Dozens, seconds to a minute in total Every PR
Messaging Kafka listener + broker, idempotency, DLT A few Every PR
External HTTP clients against WireMock: errors, retries, timeouts A few per client Every PR
Contract Each API and event boundary Per consumer Every PR
E2E A handful of critical journeys through the gateway Few, minutes Before release
Performance Baseline with thresholds; full load test Few Nightly, pre-release
Production Smoke after deploy, canary, synthetic checks Continuous After deploy

Principles. Test behaviour through public interfaces. Use real infrastructure where the database or broker's behaviour is part of what you are checking. Mock only at boundaries you do not control. Keep the PR build under 10 minutes or people stop running it. Each bug gets a regression test first. Tests are production code: reviewed and refactored. Delete tests that provide no signal.

30.16 Interview questions and answers

Q1. Testing pyramid vs testing trophy: which do you follow?

It depends on where the complexity is. A pure engine with many rules gets a pyramid of unit tests; a CRUD service gets mostly integration tests, because a mock of the repository would verify nothing. What I hold constant is the goal: the most confidence per minute of build time, and tests that survive refactoring.

Q2. What is the difference between JUnit 4 and JUnit 5?

JUnit 5 is modular (Platform, Jupiter, Vintage), with composable extensions instead of a single @RunWith, @BeforeEach and @BeforeAll naming, parameterized and nested tests built in, lambdas in assertThrows and assertAll, and package-private test classes and methods. assert message goes last, not first.

Q3. How many instances of a test class does JUnit 5 create?

One per test method by default, so instance fields are fresh for each test. @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS) shares one instance, which allows non-static @BeforeAll and @MethodSource but risks state leaking between tests.

Q4. What is the output order, and how many times does each run for two test methods?

@BeforeAll once, then for each test: constructor, @BeforeEach, the test, @AfterEach; then @AfterAll once. With two tests the constructor runs twice. @AfterEach runs even when a test fails, unless the instance was never constructed.

Q5. assertAll vs several assertEquals?

Consecutive assertions stop at the first failure; assertAll runs all of them and reports every failure together. AssertJ's SoftAssertions does the same. Useful when checking several fields of one result.

Q6. How do you write a parameterized test, and with which sources?

@ParameterizedTest with @ValueSource (one literal argument), @CsvSource (rows inline), @CsvFileSource, @EnumSource, @MethodSource (a static factory for complex objects), @NullAndEmptySource, or a custom @ArgumentsSource. Boundary tables suit it perfectly: each row names a rule.

Q7. What is a JUnit 5 extension?

A class implementing callback interfaces (BeforeEachCallback, ParameterResolver, TestWatcher, InvocationInterceptor) registered through @ExtendWith or @RegisterExtension. It is how Spring, Mockito and Testcontainers integrate. Several can be combined, which JUnit 4's single runner did not allow.

Q8. Mock vs stub vs spy vs fake?

A stub gives canned answers. A mock also records calls, so that you can verify them. A spy wraps a real object and lets you override some methods. A fake is a working simplified implementation (an in-memory repository). Mockito's mock() can be used as either stub or mock; the distinction is about what the test asserts.

Q9. Why does this spy test throw?

List<String> spy = spy(new ArrayList<>());
when(spy.get(0)).thenReturn("x");     // IndexOutOfBoundsException

when(spy.get(0)) calls the real get(0) on an empty list before stubbing takes effect. Use doReturn("x").when(spy).get(0), which does not invoke the method.

Q10. How do @Mock, @InjectMocks and @Spy work, and what goes wrong?

MockitoExtension creates mocks and injects them into the @InjectMocks instance, trying the biggest constructor, then setters, then fields. Injection failures are silent: if a constructor cannot be satisfied, a dependency may just be null, so a plain new Service(mockA, mockB) is often clearer and fails at compile time when the signature changes.

Q11. any() matcher pitfalls?

If one argument uses a matcher, all must: verify(x).send(any(), "literal") throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException; use eq("literal"). any(String.class) does not match null since Mockito 2, and any() does. ArgumentCaptor is better than a loose matcher when you want to inspect the argument afterwards.

Q12. Can Mockito mock static and final methods? Should you?

Yes: since Mockito 5 the inline mock maker is the default, so final is automatic and mockStatic works, scoped to a thread and a try block. Prefer not to need them: inject a Clock, wrap a static SDK behind an interface. Reach for it on legacy code that you cannot yet change.

Q13. When should you not mock?

Value objects, types you do not own (JdbcTemplate, RestClient, KafkaTemplate), and when the real thing is cheap. If a test mocks everything and asserts the stubs, it proves nothing. Over-mocking is the top reason that suites pass while production fails and refactors break tests.

Q14. verify vs state assertions: when do you use each?

Assert returned values or stored state where possible, because that is behaviour. Use verify for outgoing commands whose effect is outside the unit: an event published, an email sent. Verifying internal query calls couples the test to the implementation.

Q15. What are Spring Boot test slices and why use them?

Annotations that load only a layer of the context: @WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest, @RestClientTest. They start quicker and force focus. Beans outside the slice must be mocked, or imported with @Import. Beware that @Components used in the slice's filters or config can stop the context loading, which is a common surprise with a global @EnableX on the main class.

Q16. @WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest with MockMvc?

@WebMvcTest loads the web layer with mocks for services, so it tests validation, status codes, JSON and security in isolation. @SpringBootTest with @AutoConfigureMockMvc loads everything but still no real HTTP server. webEnvironment=RANDOM_PORT starts Tomcat for real, using TestRestTemplate or WebTestClient; it runs on a different thread, so a @Transactional test no longer rolls back what the server did.

Q17. Why might @DataJpaTest pass with H2 and fail in production?

H2 is another database: jsonb, partial indexes, ON CONFLICT, SKIP LOCKED behaviour, window function details, and constraint timing differ, and Flyway migrations with PostgreSQL syntax may not even run. Use @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = NONE) with PostgreSQL (Testcontainers or embedded). A test against the wrong engine gives false confidence.

Q18. What are the risks of @Transactional on a test?

The test's transaction wraps the code under test and rolls back, so commits never happen: after-commit listeners do not fire, REQUIRED methods join instead of behaving as in production, LazyInitializationException is hidden because the session stays open, Hibernate may never flush (so a constraint violation goes unseen unless you call flush()), and other threads cannot see the data. Use it for simple repository tests, and avoid it where transactions are the behaviour under test.

Q19. How does Spring test context caching work, and how do you speed up a slow suite?

Contexts are cached per JVM by a key of configuration: classes, profiles, properties, mock beans. Reuse is automatic for identical keys. The killers: varied @MockitoBean sets, many @TestPropertySource variations and @DirtiesContext. Standardise on one or two base classes, replace full-context tests with slices, parallelise with surefire forks, and check for caching misses in logs.

Q20. @MockBean vs @Mock, and what changed in Spring Boot 3.4?

@Mock creates a Mockito mock in a plain unit test with no Spring. @MockBean puts a mock into the application context, replacing any bean of that type, and changes the context cache key. In Boot 3.4 it is deprecated in favour of Spring Framework 6.2's @MockitoBean (and @MockitoSpyBean for @SpyBean).

Q21. What does Testcontainers give over an in-memory DB, and what does it cost?

The real engine, real SQL, real extensions, real locks, so tests find real bugs. Costs: Docker on all machines, container start time (a few seconds), and CI configuration. Reduce it through singleton containers, and reusable containers locally. Embedded-binary options like Zonky avoid Docker altogether, as we chose.

Q22. What is @ServiceConnection?

A Boot 3.1+ annotation on a container field that generates ConnectionDetails beans, so the app connects to the container without manual @DynamicPropertySource. Boot detects the type (PostgreSQL, Kafka, Redis, and more). You still use @DynamicPropertySource for anything without a connection-details factory, such as a custom issuer URI.

Q23. How would you test a Kafka consumer?

A fast logic test by calling the listener method directly, plus an integration test through a real broker (@EmbeddedKafka or Testcontainers) so that deserialization, the error handler and commits run. Assert with Awaitility. Include a duplicate, a poison message, a DLT case and a rollback case. Use unique topics or group ids per test class to avoid interference.

Q24. How do you assert that something did not happen asynchronously?

Do not sleep and hope. Send a marker message after the event in the same partition, wait until the marker is processed, then assert the state: order within a partition guarantees that the earlier message has been handled. For non-partitioned flows, Awaitility's during(...) asserts that the condition holds for a period.

Q25. How do you test an outbox relay?

Insert business data and check the outbox row in the same transaction; roll back and check it is gone. With a mock or failing KafkaTemplate, check that the batch stops at the first failure, that attempts and last_error are updated, and later rows stay unsent, then that the next tick retries the oldest. Run two relays concurrently to prove SKIP LOCKED prevents a double send. End to end, check that a real consumer receives events in order.

Q26. What is contract testing, and why not just end-to-end?

Each side is verified separately against a shared contract: the consumer against a stub, the provider by replaying the contract. It catches breaking changes in that repo's build, quickly, without deploying the whole system. E2E tests are slow, flaky and fail far from the cause. Contracts check shape, not business logic, so you still need a few E2E tests of the critical paths.

Q27. Pact vs Spring Cloud Contract?

Pact is consumer-driven and polyglot, with a broker and can-i-deploy. Spring Cloud Contract is usually provider-written, generates provider tests and a WireMock stub jar, and fits all-Spring shops. Choose Pact when consumers are diverse or external teams; SCC when one org controls JVM services.

Q28. WireMock vs MockRestServiceServer vs mocking the client?

Mocking the client interface tests only your logic. MockRestServiceServer intercepts at the RestTemplate/RestClient level with no real socket, which is fast and good for mapping. WireMock is a real HTTP server, so timeouts, connection resets, slow responses and real client configuration are all exercised. Use the latter for resilience behaviour.

Q29. How would you test a Paddle webhook endpoint?

Build the raw body and sign it with the test secret. Cases: a valid signature is processed; a wrong signature, a missing header or an expired timestamp are refused; the same event id twice changes nothing; a failure in processing returns 500 and rolls back so that a retry works; an out-of-order event is tolerated; a parse failure does not trigger an endless retry. Use real recorded payloads as fixtures.

Q30. How do you test Spring Security rules?

spring-security-test with jwt() or @WithMockUser in MockMvc. Test a matrix of roles against endpoint groups, starting with denials: 401 for anonymous, 403 for wrong role, wrong-tenant access refused. Test method security through the proxy (a bean, not new). Test converters that map claims to authorities with real token shapes, and CSRF rules where relevant.

Q31. How do you test multi-tenant isolation?

Create two tenants with data. For each endpoint, access A's resource as B and expect 403 or 404, never a 200. Generate these tests from the endpoint catalogue where possible, so that new endpoints are covered by default. Check background jobs and caches also, because they are where tenant context gets lost.

Q32. How do you test a race condition?

Make it likely and make the result checkable: real database, multiple threads released together by a CountDownLatch, many repetitions, assert invariants such as no duplicates. For determinism, force the exact interleaving with two transactions and latches. Do not mark the test @Transactional. A pass does not prove absence; a good design (database constraints) helps more than a test.

Q33. How do you test SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED claims?

Against the real engine. Insert N rows, call claim from two threads released together, then assert the union size is N with no duplicates. Then assert that a second claim returns nothing, because claimed rows are marked. Also test crash recovery: a claim with an expired heartbeat gets reclaimed. That's the shape of our twoInstancesNeverClaimTheSameJob.

Q34. How do you test optimistic locking?

Load the same entity in two transactions, commit the first, and assert ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException on the second. Use TransactionTemplate rather than @Transactional on the test, so that each commit truly happens. Then test the caller's reaction: a retry or a 409.

Q35. How do you test a time-dependent feature?

Inject a java.time.Clock, with Clock.fixed in tests, or a mutable test clock that you advance. Cover the awkward dates: midnight, month end, leap day, DST transitions, and a non-UTC default zone. Never compare to Instant.now() in tests; never Thread.sleep through a TTL.

Q36. How do you test scheduled jobs?

Call the method directly in the test instead of waiting for the trigger; test the schedule separately with CronExpression.parse(...).next(...). Disable schedulers in the test context with a property so that they do not interfere. For distributed behaviour, run two instances concurrently against the same database.

Q37. Load vs stress vs soak vs spike test?

Load: does it meet SLOs at the expected peak? Stress: where and how does it break, and does it recover? Spike: does a sudden burst cause a meltdown? Soak: do leaks show up over many hours (heap, connections, disk)? Each answers a different question and usually finds different bugs.

Q38. JMeter vs Gatling vs k6?

JMeter: mature and protocol-rich, GUI and XML, thread-per-user is heavy. Gatling: code DSL in Java, Scala or Kotlin, async engine, good reports and assertions for CI. k6: JavaScript scripting with a Go runtime, thresholds fail the build. In a Java team I would use Gatling; for quick scripting k6.

Q39. What is coordinated omission?

A load generator that waits for a response before sending the next request slows down when the server stalls, so the requests that would have suffered are never sent and the latency percentiles look far better than reality. Use an open workload model with a fixed arrival rate, and tools that correct for it (Gatling's open injection, wrk2, HdrHistogram correction).

Q40. Your load test shows p99 at 5 s but the app looks idle. Where do you look?

At a saturated bottleneck with no CPU: Hikari pending connections, a blocked thread pool (take a thread dump), database locks, GC pauses, DNS or TLS on new connections, a throttled CPU limit, or the load generator itself being the bottleneck. Correlate with traces to see which hop owns the time.

Q41. What is mutation testing, and what does it reveal that coverage does not?

PIT changes the code slightly and reruns the tests; surviving mutants mean no test noticed. Coverage only shows that a line ran, not that anything checked the result: a test with no assertions gets 100% coverage and 0% mutation score. It is expensive, so target critical logic and use incremental analysis.

Q42. What code coverage target do you set?

No universal number. I look at trends, at diff coverage on new code, and at what is uncovered, particularly error paths and money logic. A hard 90% gate generates worthless tests of getters. Coverage is a good negative indicator: uncovered code is definitely untested, but covered code is not necessarily tested.

Q43. What causes flaky tests, and how do you deal with them?

Timing and sleeps, shared state and order dependence, real clocks and time zones, unordered results, port conflicts, external services, and real production races. Track flakiness, quarantine with an owner, then fix the cause: Awaitility, data isolation, injected clocks, ORDER BY. Blanket retries hide the bugs. A flaky test can be the only signal of a real race, so investigate first.

Q44. How do you keep tests independent when they share a database?

Each test creates its own data with unique ids (a fresh org per test works very well in a multi-tenant system) and queries only that. Alternatively use a new schema per class or truncate between tests. Avoid relying on a shared seed that tests mutate, and avoid global counts in assertions.

Q45. What is a test data builder and why use one?

A fluent object with valid defaults: aRun().failed().forOrg(x).build(). Tests state only the relevant fields, so adding a field changes one builder rather than hundreds of tests. Object Mother (named factories such as Runs.completed()) is a simpler variation; both beat copying constructors or shared SQL scripts.

Q46. TDD: do you practise it? When does it not help?

For rule-heavy logic, a bug fix or a parser: yes, because the tests drive a clean API and a failing test first proves the bug. It helps less in exploratory spikes and thin glue code, where you first need to learn the shape of the answer. Honest answer: I write tests first when I know what correct means.

Q47. What does BDD add, and is Cucumber worth it?

BDD focuses tests on behaviour in shared language. Given/When/Then structure and method names are always worth it. Cucumber is only worth it if business people truly read or write the scenarios; otherwise it is a costly regex layer between two developers.

Q48. How do you test an LLM feature when the output is non-deterministic?

Separate the layers. Deterministic parts (prompt building, parsing, retries, business logic) use a stubbed LlmClient with exact assertions. Model quality is measured statistically with a golden dataset and scoring rules on prompt or model change, gated on a threshold compared with a baseline. Assert properties such as valid JSON or a chosen column existing, not exact text.

Q49. What is a golden dataset, and how do you maintain it?

A curated set of real, anonymised inputs with expected outputs or scoring criteria, representing common cases and known failures. Each production mistake becomes a new case. Version it with the prompts, track per-case and aggregate scores over time, and review it periodically because the domain drifts. Do not tune prompts on the entire set, or you will overfit it; keep a holdout.

Q50. How do you test for prompt injection and hallucination regressions?

An adversarial dataset: documents with embedded instructions, requests for other tenants' data. Assert on outcomes: no tool call outside the tenant, no secret in the output. For hallucination, check grounding: cited values must exist in the source, totals must match, and invented column names must be rejected by the validator. Code-level checks are the real defence; tests make sure that they stay.

Q51. How do you test a retry and circuit breaker configuration?

Against WireMock or a stubbed client: N failures then success gives N+1 calls; 4xx not retried; back-off observed using a test clock or a registry event; breaker opens after the threshold, fails fast without calling, half-opens after the wait and closes. Resilience4j exposes registries and events to assert. Also test the fallback's response, not only that it gets called.

Q52. How do you test Flyway migrations?

Run all migrations from empty in every integration test run (the context start does this), then ddl-auto=validate so Hibernate checks that entities match the schema. For risky data migrations, load a representative fixture at the previous version, run the new migration with flyway.target control, and assert the data. Rehearse on a production-sized copy for lock and duration.

Q53. What would you do with a 45-minute build?

Measure before changing: per-class times and the context count. Usually the fixes are reducing context variation, moving logic tests from @SpringBootTest to unit tests, sharing containers, parallel forks, and building only what changed. Split out the slow suites to nightly if they rarely find anything. Target under 10 minutes on a PR, because a slow build makes people batch their changes, which makes everything riskier.

Q54. How do you test a service that depends on five others?

In its own build: WireMock or stub jars for those five, verified by contract tests so that stubs do not drift. A small number of tests against a shared environment or an E2E run cover the integration. Do not start all five in a developer's test run, as that is the distributed monolith of testing.

Q55. Should you test private methods?

No: test through the public API. If a private method is complex enough to need direct tests, it is probably a class waiting to be extracted. @VisibleForTesting and reflection couple tests to the structure you want to be free to change.

Q56. What do you test in a controller versus a service?

Controller: HTTP concerns — routing, validation, status codes, error envelope, serialization, authorization. Service: business rules, state transitions, transaction outcomes. A controller test that re-tests business rules, or a service test that thinks about JSON, is in the wrong place. GlobalExceptionHandler mapping is tested once, in a web slice.

Q57. How do you test against production safely?

Smoke tests after deploy with a dedicated test tenant, synthetic probes of key journeys, canaries with automated SLO checks, feature flags to expose code to internal users first, shadow traffic with side effects disabled. Keep test data clearly labelled and excluded from reporting. Our server_smoke.py is read-only by design.

Q58. Describe your project's testing strategy in an interview.

"Unit tests are dense where logic is: the expression language and the match engine. Every service runs integration tests on a real PostgreSQL, using an embedded binary with the real Flyway migrations, so that SQL like SKIP LOCKED and ON CONFLICT is tested for real. Concurrency has explicit tests, for example two threads claiming jobs must not overlap. External calls use stubbed HTTP. An end-to-end script goes through the gateway, and a performance stage asserts exact match counts against a baseline, since in reconciliation a fast wrong answer is the worst failure. What I would add with a team: contract tests between services and Testcontainers-based Kafka tests per service."
